Let $\tilde{R}$ be a different component of $(\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\setminus\Omega_{j})\cap\Omega$ . Then we claim $\partial\tilde{R}\cap\overline{R}^{\prime}=\varnothing$ . Indeed, if not $\tilde{R}$ would be on the opposite side of a disk in $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ from $R^{\prime}$ . Since $R^{\prime}\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ and (by fact (1) above) $\tilde{R}\cap\tilde{\Omega}=\varnothing$ , we reach a contradiction. Hence, we can iterate the above procedure and conclude by induction. ∎

#### 7.5. Application 3: Decomposing stacks

In the case of positive prescribing function, we will decompose stacked disk minimization problems into small stacked disk minimization problems each with 1 or 2 disks.

We first separate stacks consisting of 1 disk.

#### Lemma 7.8.

Suppose $D_{1}$ is oriented up. Let $D_{1}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[D_{1}]$ so that $D_{1}^{\prime}$ has transverse intersections with each $D_{i}$ . For any $\varepsilon>0$ , there is a $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ satisfying

$$ \Sigma\triangle\Sigma^{\prime}\subset U, $$

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime}\cap U)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{1}^{\prime})+\sum_{i=2}^{n}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{i})+\varepsilon, $$

and

$$ \mathbb{M}(T(\Sigma,\Sigma^{\prime})-([\Omega_{1}]-[\Omega_{1}^{\prime}])+2[\Omega_{1}\setminus(\Omega\cup\Omega_{1}^{\prime})])\leq\varepsilon. $$

#### Proof.

We apply Lemma 7.3 to $\{D_{1}^{\prime}\}\cup\{D_{i}\}_{i=2}^{n}$ . The resulting disks satisfy (7.12) as in the first step of the proof of Lemma 7.7. However, we have $[(\Omega_{1}^{\prime}\setminus\Omega_{1})\cap\Omega]=0$ because $D_{1}$ is oriented up. Hence, the result follows from Lemma 7.5. ∎

Now we separate stacks consisting of 2 disks.

#### Lemma 7.9.

Suppose $D_{j}$ is oriented down and $D_{j+1}$ is oriented up. Let $D_{j}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[D_{j}]$ and $D_{j+1}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[D_{j+1}]$ be mutually disjoint and have transverse intersections with each $D_{i}$ . For any $\varepsilon>0$ , there is a $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ satisfying

$$ \Sigma\triangle\Sigma^{\prime}\subset U, $$

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime}\cap U)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j}^{\prime})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j+1}^{\prime})+\sum_{i\notin\{j,j+1\}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{i})+\varepsilon, $$

and

$$ \mathbb{M}(T(\Sigma,\Sigma^{\prime})-(([\Omega_{j}]+[\Omega_{j+1}])-([\Omega_{j}^{\prime}]+[\Omega_{j+1}^{\prime}]))+2[\Omega_{j}\cup\Omega_{j+1}\setminus(\Omega\cup\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\cup\Omega_{j+1}^{\prime})])\leq\varepsilon. $$

#### Proof.

We apply Lemma 7.3 to the disks $\{D_{j}^{\prime},D_{j+1}^{\prime}\}\cup\{D_{i}\}_{i\neq j,j+1}$ , producing new disks $\{\tilde{D}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ .

We compute

$$ \displaystyle[\Omega]-[\tilde{\Omega}] \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\Omega_{i}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\tilde{\Omega}_{i}] \displaystyle=([\Omega_{j}]+[\Omega_{j+1}])-([\Omega_{j}^{\prime}]-[\Omega_{j+1}^{\prime}]) \displaystyle\hskip 11.38092pt+\left([\Omega_{j}^{\prime}]+[\Omega_{j+1}^{\prime}]+\sum_{i\neq j,j+1}[\Omega_{i}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\tilde{\Omega}_{i}]\right). $$

Let

$$ \tilde{N}\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}_{\tilde{\Omega}_{i}},\ \ N^{\prime}\coloneqq\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{j}^{\prime}}+\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{j+1}^{\prime}}+\sum_{i\neq j,j+1}\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{i}}. $$

To show (7.20), it suffices to show for $x\in U\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{D}_{i}$ that

$$ N^{\prime}(x)-\tilde{N}(x)=\begin{cases}-2&x\in(\Omega_{j}\cup\Omega_{j+1})\setminus(\Omega\cup\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\cup\Omega_{j+1}^{\prime})\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Let $R$ be the component of $U\setminus\bigcup_{i}D_{i}$ containing $x$ . Let $x_{0}\in C\cap\overline{R}$ . Let $\gamma:(0,1]\to U$ be a path in $R$ so that

- • $\gamma$ avoids $\Gamma_{k}$ ,

- • $\gamma$ has transverse intersection with $D_{j}^{\prime}$ and $D_{j+1}^{\prime}$ ,

- • $\lim_{t\to 0}\gamma(t)=x_{0}$ and $\gamma(1)=x$ .

We have $N^{\prime}(x_{0})=\tilde{N}(x_{0})$ . Along subsequent intersections of $\gamma$ with $D_{j}^{\prime}\cup D_{j+1}^{\prime}$ , each of $N^{\prime}$ and $\tilde{N}$ will increase and decrease by 1 in alternating order.

If $\gamma$ has an even number of intersections with $D_{j}^{\prime}\cup D_{j+1}^{\prime}$ , then we see $N^{\prime}(x)=\tilde{N}(x)$ . Hence, we only need to consider the case of an odd number of intersections, which is equivalent to $x\in(\Omega_{j}\cup\Omega_{j+1})\triangle(\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\cup\Omega_{j+1}^{\prime})$ . In this case, $N^{\prime}$ increases at the first intersection if and only if $x\in\Omega_{j}^{\prime}\cup\Omega_{j+1}^{\prime}$ . Note that $\tilde{N}$ decreases at the first intersection if and only if $R\subset\Omega$ . We also note that if $x\notin\Omega_{j}\cup\Omega_{j+1}$ , then $x\notin\Omega$ (by the specification of the orientations of $D_{j}$ and $D_{j+1}$ ). Hence, (7.21) follows.

The result now follows from Lemma 7.5. ∎

### 8. Replacement

We adapt the replacement theorem [AS79, Theorem 1] to the prescribed mean curvature setting. This lemma allows us to bring components of a minimizing surface outside a small ball into the ball.

To prove the replacement theorem, we first require an isoperimetric inequality.

Let $\delta$ and $c_{1}$ be the constants from Lemma 4.2, and let

$$ \eta\coloneqq\min\left\{\frac{\mathcal{H}^{3}(M)}{2},\ \frac{1}{8c^{3}c_{1}^{2}},\ c_{1}\delta^{3}\right\}. $$

#### Proposition 8.1.

If $\Omega\subset M$ is a set of finite perimeter with $\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega)\leq\eta$ , then

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega)\leq c_{1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial\Omega)^{3/2}, $$

and

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega)\geq\mathcal{A}^{c}(\Omega)\geq\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial\Omega). $$

#### Proof.

If $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial\Omega)\geq\delta^{2}$ , then (8.2) holds trivially by the definition of $\eta$ . On the other hand, if $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial\Omega)<\delta^{2}$ , Lemma 4.2 directly implies (8.2). Then (8.3) follows, as we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{c}(\Omega)=\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial\Omega)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega) \displaystyle\geq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial\Omega)(1-cc_{1}^{2/3}\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega)^{1/3})\geq\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial\Omega). $$

The bound $\mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega)\geq\mathcal{A}^{c}(\Omega)$ holds because $h\leq c$ . ∎

We are now equipped to prove the replacement theorem.

#### Lemma 8.2 (Replacement).

Let $\xi>0$ . Suppose $\mathcal{H}^{3}(U)\leq\eta$ . Let $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ . Then there exists $\tilde{\Sigma}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ and an open subset $B\subset U$ with $\overline{B}\cap\tilde{\Sigma}=\varnothing$ such that

$$ (\tilde{\Sigma}\cup\partial B)\cap U_{\xi}=\Sigma\cap U_{\xi}, $$

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+T_{h}(\Sigma,\tilde{\Sigma})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+T_{h}(\Sigma,\tilde{\Sigma})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(B)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma), $$

and there is a set of disjoint oriented disks $\mathcal{S}$ with

$$ [\tilde{\Sigma}]\llcorner U=\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}}[D]. $$

Suppose additionally that

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime})+T_{h}(\Sigma,\Sigma^{\prime})+\varepsilon $$

for all $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ . Then

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime})+T_{h}(\tilde{\Sigma},\Sigma^{\prime})+\varepsilon $$

for all $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\tilde{\Sigma}]$ , and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}((\Sigma\triangle\tilde{\Sigma})\cap U_{\xi})\leq 2\varepsilon. $$

Let $P\subset\Sigma\cap U$ be a union of components of $\Sigma\cap U$ . Let $\mathcal{S}_{P}\subset\mathcal{S}$ be the collection of disks $D\in\mathcal{S}$ with $D\cap U_{\xi}\subset P$ , and let $\tilde{P}\coloneqq\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}D$ . Then

$$ \mathcal{H}^{1}\Big(\overline{\tilde{P}}\cap\partial U\Big)\leq\mathcal{H}^{1}(\overline{P}\cap\partial U) $$

and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(P)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{P})+2\varepsilon. $$

#### Proof.

We use the same replacement procedure as in the proof of [AS79, Theorem 1]. However, we have to keep track of relative volumes, so we include the details of the procedure before the smoothing, perturbation, and induction steps.

Let $\Lambda$ be any component of $\Sigma\setminus U$ such that $\Lambda\cap\partial\Sigma=\varnothing$ . By Lemma 4.3, there is a unique compact set $K_{\Lambda}\subset M\setminus U$ satisfying (4.13) and (4.14. Given any component $\Lambda^{\prime}$ of $\Sigma\setminus U$ with $\Lambda^{\prime}\subset K_{\Lambda}$ , we have $\Lambda^{\prime}\cap\partial\Sigma=\varnothing$ and $K_{\Lambda^{\prime}}\subset K_{\Lambda}$ (by the assumption on $U$ and $\Sigma$ ). Hence, we can select a component $\Lambda$ of $\Sigma\setminus U$ such that $\Lambda\cap\partial\Sigma=\varnothing$ and $\mathrm{int}(K_{\Lambda})\cap\Sigma=\varnothing$ .

Let $\chi$ be a diffeomorphism of $\mathbb{D}$ onto $\Sigma$ , and consider the set $H\coloneqq\chi^{-1}(\Lambda)$ . $H$ is a compact connected subset of $\mathbb{D}$ bounded by a finite collection of pairwise disjoint smooth Jordan curves $\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{n}$ . Suppose without loss of generality that $\gamma_{1}$ is the outermost of the curves. By the connectedness of $H$ , we can write

$$ H=\overline{\mathrm{int}\gamma_{1}}\setminus\bigcup_{j=2}^{n}\mathrm{int}\gamma_{j}. $$

Recall that $F=\partial K_{\Lambda}\cap\partial U$ . Define $F_{1}\subset F$ to be the component of $F$ which contains the Jordan curve $\chi(\gamma_{1})$ , and $F_{2}\coloneqq F\setminus F_{1}$ . Define $I\coloneqq\cup\mathrm{int}\gamma_{j}$ , where the union is over those $j$ such that $\chi(\gamma_{j})\subset F_{2}$ . Let $\Lambda_{2}\coloneqq\chi(I)$ . Then $\Lambda_{1}\coloneqq\Lambda\cup\Lambda_{2}$ is diffeomorphic to the connected subset $H\cup I$ of $\mathbb{D}$ , and $\partial\Lambda_{1}=\partial F_{1}$ . By [AS79, Lemma 1], we can construct a diffeomorphism $\alpha$ of $\Lambda_{1}$ onto $F_{1}$ such that $\alpha$ coincides with the identity on $\partial\Lambda_{1}=\partial F_{1}$ . We define a Lipschitz map $\hat{\chi}:\mathbb{D}\to M$ by

$$ \hat{\chi}(x)\coloneqq\begin{cases}(\alpha\circ\chi)(x)&x\in H\cup I\\
\chi(x)&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

We consider the following two cases:

Case 1: $\partial\Sigma\cap(F_{1}\setminus\partial F_{1})=\varnothing$ . Since $\mathrm{int}(K_{\Lambda})\cap\Sigma=\varnothing$ , $\hat{\chi}$ is injective, and we define

$$ \tilde{\Sigma}\coloneqq\hat{\chi}(\mathbb{D})=(\Sigma\setminus\Lambda_{1})\cup F_{1}. $$

Let $V_{\Lambda}\subset U\cup\bigcup_{\Lambda^{\prime}}K_{\Lambda^{\prime}}$ be the unique open set bounded by $\Lambda_{1}\cup F_{1}$ . Note that $\mathrm{int}(K_{\Lambda})\subset V_{\Lambda}$ , so $V_{\Lambda}$ is on the outside of $F_{1}$ . Let $B\coloneqq V_{\Lambda}\cap U$ , $V_{\Lambda}^{o}\coloneqq V_{\Lambda}\setminus\overline{U}$ , $\Lambda_{1}^{i}\coloneqq\Lambda_{1}\cap U$ , $\Lambda_{1}^{o}=\Lambda_{1}\setminus\overline{U}$ , and $G\coloneqq V_{\Lambda}\cap\partial U$ . Since $V_{\Lambda}$ is on the outside of $F_{1}$ , we have $\partial B=\Lambda_{1}^{i}\cup G$ . Our goal is to show

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(V_{\Lambda})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(B)<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma). $$

We have $\partial V_{\Lambda}^{o}=\Lambda_{1}^{o}\cup F_{1}\cup G$ , so (4.14) implies

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{1})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(G)<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Lambda_{1}^{o})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(V_{\Lambda}^{o}). $$

By the definition of $\tilde{\Sigma}$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})=\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Lambda_{1})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{1}). $$

Hence, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(V_{\Lambda})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(B) \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Lambda_{1}^{o})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{1})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(V_{\Lambda}^{o})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(G) \displaystyle<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma). $$

Case 2: $\partial\Sigma\cap(F_{1}\setminus\partial F_{1})\neq\varnothing$ . Since $\mathrm{int}(K_{\Lambda})\cap\Sigma=\varnothing$ , we have $\partial\Sigma\subset F_{1}\setminus\partial F_{1}$ in this case. Hence, $\hat{\chi}^{-1}(\partial\Sigma)=\partial\mathbb{D}\cup\gamma$ , where $\gamma$ is a smooth Jordan curve in $\mathbb{D}\setminus\partial\mathbb{D}$ . We define

$$ \tilde{\Sigma}\coloneqq\hat{\chi}(\mathrm{int}\gamma)\subset F_{1}. $$

Let $V_{\Lambda}\subset U\cup\bigcup_{\Lambda^{\prime}}K_{\Lambda^{\prime}}$ be the unique open set bounded by $\Sigma$ and $\tilde{\Sigma}$ . Note that $\mathrm{int}(K_{\Lambda})\subset V_{\Lambda}$ , so $V_{\Lambda}$ is on the outside of $\tilde{\Sigma}$ . Let $B\coloneqq V_{\Lambda}\cap U$ , $V_{\Lambda}^{o}\coloneqq V_{\Lambda}\setminus\overline{U}$ , $\Sigma^{i}\coloneqq\Sigma\cap U$ , $\Sigma^{o}\coloneqq\Sigma\setminus\overline{U}$ , and $G\coloneqq V_{\Lambda}\cap\partial U$ . Since $V_{\Lambda}$ is on the outside of $\tilde{\Sigma}$ , we have $\partial B=\Sigma^{i}\cup G$ . Our goal is to show

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(V_{\Lambda})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(B)<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma). $$

We have $\partial V_{\Lambda}^{o}=\Sigma^{o}\cup\tilde{\Sigma}\cup G$ , so (4.14) implies

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(G)<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{o})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(V_{\Lambda}^{o}). $$

Hence, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(V_{\Lambda})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(B) \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(V_{\Lambda}^{o})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{i})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(G) \displaystyle<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma). $$

The smoothing, slight perturbation, and induction steps now follow exactly as in the proof of [AS79, Theorem 1] (with the additional observation that small perturbations make small changes to relative volumes). Taking $B$ to be the union of the perturbations of the sets $B$ from each iteration applied to the perturbed $\tilde{\Sigma}$ from the previous step, we obtain (8.4) and (8.6) immediately. Moreover, by (8.12) and (8.13), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma})+c|T(\Sigma,\tilde{\Sigma})|+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(B)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma). $$

Since

$$ T_{h}(\Sigma,\tilde{\Sigma})\leq c|T(\Sigma,\tilde{\Sigma})|, $$

the second inequality in (8.5) holds. The first inequality in (8.5) follows from (8.3) and the fact that $B\subset U$ .

(8.8) follows from (8.5), (8.7), Proposition 5.3, and the fact that $\mathcal{D}(U)[\tilde{\Sigma}]\subset\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ .

To prove (8.9), we note that

$$ \Sigma\triangle\tilde{\Sigma}\cap U_{\xi}=\partial B\cap U_{\xi}. $$

By (8.5) and (8.7) with $\Sigma^{\prime}=\tilde{\Sigma}$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(B)\leq\varepsilon. $$

By (8.3), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B)\leq 2\varepsilon, $$

which implies (8.9).

(8.10) follows from the construction of $\tilde{\Sigma}$ ; namely, for each component of $\Sigma\cap U$ , either (1) it is thrown away in $\partial B$ , or (2) each component of its intersection with $\partial U$ is either (a) kept unchanged, or (b) pushed away from $\partial U$ in the perturbation step.

(8.11) follows from the construction of $\tilde{\Sigma}$ and (8.9); namely, each component of $\Sigma\cap U$ is either (1) thrown away in $\partial B$ , whose area is at most $2\varepsilon$ by (8.9), or (2) kept and given potentially larger area (by adding pieces of $\partial U$ ). ∎

### 9. Filigree

We adapt the filigree lemma [AS79, Lemma 3] to the prescribed mean curvature setting. This lemma allows us to ignore small area components of a minimizing sequence in small balls. Let $U$ and $\theta$ be chosen (and $\beta$ and $\delta_{1}$ be thereby defined) as in §5.1, and let $\eta$ be defined as in (8.1).

#### Lemma 9.1 (Filigree).

Suppose $\mathcal{H}^{3}(U(\theta))\leq\eta$ . Let $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(U(\theta))$ satisfy

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial U(\theta))+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma\setminus U)\leq\delta_{1}^{2}/32 $$

and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime})+T_{h}(\Sigma,\Sigma^{\prime})+\varepsilon $$

for all $\Sigma^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma]$ . Let $P$ be a union of some components of $\Sigma\cap U(\theta)$ . If

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(P)\leq\frac{\theta^{2}}{48\beta} $$

then

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(P\cap U)\leq 6\varepsilon. $$

#### Proof.

For almost every $\sigma\in[0,\theta]$ , we have $\Sigma\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(U(\sigma))$ . Choose any such $\sigma=t\theta$ for $t\in[0,1]$ . We apply Lemma 8.2 to $\Sigma$ in $U(\sigma)$ with some small constant $\xi$ , yielding $\tilde{\Sigma}$ .

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the set of disks composing $\tilde{\Sigma}$ in $U(\sigma)$ . Let $\mathcal{S}_{P}\subset\mathcal{S}$ be the set of disks $D\in\mathcal{S}$ so that $D\cap U(\sigma)_{\xi}\subset P$ . Let $\tilde{P}\coloneqq\bigcup_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}D$ . Take a disk $D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}$ . Let $F_{D}$ denote the isoperimetric region in $\partial U(\sigma)$ for $\partial D$ . Let $\Lambda_{D}$ denote the region in $U(\sigma)$ bounded by $D\cup F_{D}$ .

Consider the competitor $\Sigma^{\prime}$ for $\tilde{\Sigma}$ given by replacing each disk $D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}$ with $F_{D}$ , and then resolving the overlaps and perturbing using Lemma 7.6. Then

$$ T_{h}(\tilde{\Sigma},\Sigma^{\prime})\leq c\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Lambda_{D})+\varepsilon/2. $$

By (8.2), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(\Lambda_{D})^{2/3}\leq c_{1}^{2/3}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\mathcal{H}^{3}(F_{D})). $$

Hence, we have

$$ \displaystyle T_{h}(\tilde{\Sigma},\Sigma^{\prime}) \displaystyle\leq cc_{1}^{2/3}(\mathcal{H}^{3}(U(\sigma)))^{1/3}\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D}))+\varepsilon/2 \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D}))+\varepsilon/2. $$

By Lemma 8.2(8.8), we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D) \displaystyle=\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma}\cap U(\sigma)) \displaystyle\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma^{\prime}\cap U(\sigma))+T_{h}(\tilde{\Sigma},\Sigma^{\prime})+\varepsilon \displaystyle\leq\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{P}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D})+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D}))+2\varepsilon, $$

so

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{P})=\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)\leq 3\sum_{D\in\mathcal{S}_{P}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D})+4\varepsilon. $$

By the isoperimetric inequality on $\partial U(\sigma)$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{P})\leq 3\beta(\mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial\tilde{P}))^{2}+4\varepsilon. $$

By Lemma 8.2(8.10), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial\tilde{P})\leq\mathcal{H}^{1}(P\cap\partial U(\sigma)). $$

By Lemma 8.2(8.11), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(P\cap U(\sigma))\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{P})+2\varepsilon. $$

Hence, we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(P\cap U(t\theta))\leq 3\beta(\mathcal{H}^{1}(P\cap\partial U(t\theta)))^{2}+6\varepsilon. $$

Let $f(t)\coloneqq\mathcal{H}^{2}(P\cap U(t\theta))-6\varepsilon$ . Then by the coarea formula we have

$$ f\leq 3\beta\theta^{-2}(f^{\prime})^{2}. $$

Suppose without loss of generality that $f(1)>0$ . Let

$$ t_{0}\coloneqq\inf\{t\in[0,1]\mid f(t)>0\}. $$

Integrating (9.3) gives

$$ (1-t_{0})\frac{\theta}{2\sqrt{3\beta}}\leq\sqrt{f(1)}-\sqrt{f(t_{0})}\leq\sqrt{\mathcal{H}^{2}(P)}. $$

Then our area assumption gives

$$ t_{0}\geq 1-\frac{2\sqrt{3\beta}}{\theta}\sqrt{\mathcal{H}^{2}(P)}\geq\frac{1}{2}. $$

Hence, $\mathcal{H}^{2}(P\cap U)\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(P\cap U(\theta/2))\leq 6\varepsilon$ . ∎

### 10. Interior Regularity

In this section we prove the interior regularity for $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ minimizing sequences of disks, following the strategy of [AS79].

We first apply Lemma 9.1 to deduce rectifiability of the limit varifold.

#### Lemma 10.1 (Rectifiability).

Let $\{\Sigma_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ satisfy $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k})\leq\delta_{2}^{2}/64$ and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}^{\prime})+T_{h}(\Sigma_{k},\Sigma_{k}^{\prime})+\varepsilon_{k} $$

for all $\Sigma_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma_{k}]$ with $\varepsilon_{k}\to 0$ . Let $V$ be the subsequential varifold limit of $\Sigma_{k}$ in $U$ provided by Theorem 6.1. Then

$$ \Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)\geq\frac{1}{1000\beta}>0 $$

for all $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ . Moreover, $V$ is rectifiable.

#### Proof.

Rectifiability follows from the positive density lower bound by [All72, Theorem 5.5].

Let $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ . Choose $r_{0}\leq 1/2$ small enough so that $\mathcal{H}^{3}(B_{r_{0}}(x))\leq\eta$ and $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B_{r}(x))\leq\delta_{2}^{2}/64$ for all $r\leq r_{0}$ . Let $r_{i}\to 0$ with $r_{i}\leq r_{0}$ , $B_{r_{i}}(x)\subset U$ , and $\Sigma_{k}\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(B_{r_{i}}(x))$ for all $k$ and $i$ , which is guaranteed by Sard’s theorem. By Lemma 9.1 with $\theta=r_{i}/2$ , if

$$ \liminf_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}\cap B_{r_{i}}(x))\leq\frac{r_{i}^{2}}{192\beta}, $$

then

$$ \|V\|(B_{r_{i}/2}(x))\leq\liminf_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}\cap B_{r_{i}/2}(x))\leq\liminf_{k}6\varepsilon_{k}=0, $$

which contradicts $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ . Hence, by the assumption of transversality, we have

$$ \|V\|(B_{r_{i}}(x))=\lim_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}\cap B_{r_{i}}(x))\geq\frac{r_{i}^{2}}{192\beta}. $$

By the monotonicity of (6.5) for $V$ , we have

$$ \Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)\geq\frac{1}{1000\beta}, $$

as desired. ∎

We now have all the tools to use the stategy of [AS79] to deduce interior regularity.

#### Theorem 10.2.

Let $\{\Sigma_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{D}^{*}(U)$ satisfy $\sup_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}\cap U)\leq\delta_{2}^{2}/64$ and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k}^{\prime})+T_{h}(\Sigma_{k},\Sigma_{k}^{\prime})+\varepsilon_{k} $$

for all $\Sigma_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(U)[\Sigma_{k}]$ with $\varepsilon_{k}\to 0$ . Let $V$ and $\Omega$ respectively be the subsequential varifold limit of $\Sigma_{k}\cap U$ and the subsequential Caccioppoli set limit of $\Omega_{k}$ provided by Theorem 6.1. Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$ .

$V$ is an integer rectifiable varifold with $c$ -bounded first variation. For every $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ , we have $\Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)=n_{x}\in\mathbb{N}$ . If $h(x)\neq 0$ , then $n_{x}\in\{1\}\cup 2\mathbb{N}$ . For every $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ , there is a neighborhood $W_{x}$ of $x$ so that the following hold.

- • $V\llcorner G(W_{x},2)=\sum_{l=1}^{n_{x}}\mathbf{v}(N_{l},1)$ , where $N_{l}\subset W_{x}$ is a $C^{1,\alpha}$ surface with $c$ -bounded first variation. Moreover, each $N_{l}$ is on one side of $N_{l^{\prime}}$ intersecting tangentially at $x$ for any $l,\ l^{\prime}\in\{1,\ldots,n_{x}\}$ .

- • If $n_{x}=1$ , then – $\|V\|\llcorner W_{x}=|D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega}|\llcorner W_{x}$ , – $V\llcorner G(W_{x},2)=\mathbf{v}(N,1)$ , where $N\subset W_{x}$ is a smooth stable surface with prescribed mean curvature $h$ with respect to the set $\Omega\cap W_{x}$ .

- • If $h(x)\neq 0$ and $n_{y}=2n$ for all $y\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|\cap W_{x}^{\prime}$ for an open set $W_{x}^{\prime}\subset W_{x}$ containing $x$ , then $V\llcorner G(W^{\prime}_{x},2)=\mathbf{v}(N,2n)$ , where $N\subset W_{x}^{\prime}$ is a smooth stable minimal surface. Moreover, $\Omega\cap W_{x}^{\prime}=W_{x}^{\prime}\setminus N$ if $h(x)>0$ , and $\Omega\cap W_{x}^{\prime}=\varnothing$ if $h(x)<0$ .

- • If $h(x)\neq 0$ , $n_{x}=2n$ , and there is a sequence $x_{j}\to x$ with $x_{j}\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ and $n_{x_{j}}\neq 2n$ , then $n=1$ and the surfaces $N_{1},\ N_{2}\subset W_{x}$ additionally satisfy that the generalized mean curvature of $N_{1}$ points towards $N_{2}$ and vice versa.

#### Proof.

By Lemma 10.1, $V$ is rectifiable and has a uniform positive density lower bound in its support. By Theorem 6.1(6.4), $V$ has $c$ -bounded first variation.

Integer Density. We show that the density of $V$ is an integer at every $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ . Since this result concerns the infinitesimal behavior of $V$ near $x$ , we push objects to $T_{x}M$ using the exponential map $\phi_{x}$ . In $T_{x}M$ , we use the standard Euclidean metric in the geodesic normal coordinates, which is the $C^{\infty}$ limit of the pullback metric under a blow up rescaling.

First, let $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ be such that there is a tangent cone $C\in\mathrm{VarTan}(V,x)$ with $\mathrm{spt}\|C\|\subset P_{C}$ , where $P_{C}$ is a 2-plane in $T_{x}M$ (by rectifiability, this holds $\|V\|$ -almost everywhere).

Fix any $\xi>0$ .

Without loss of generality, assume $P_{C}\supset\mathrm{spt}\|C\|$ is the $x_{1}x_{2}$ -plane in $T_{x}M$ .

Let $\mu_{t}$ denote the transformation of $T_{x}M$ given by $\mu_{t}(y)=ty$ . By the definition of $C$ , there is a sequence $\{r_{j}\}\to\infty$ so that

$$ (\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})_{\#}V\rightharpoonup C $$

as $j\to\infty$ . We always assume $r_{j}\geq 1$ .

By the lower density bound from Lemma 10.1 and the monotonicity of (6.5), there is a sequence $\{\sigma_{j}\}\to 0$ so that

$$ (B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)\times(-2,2))\cap\mathrm{spt}\|(\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})_{\#}V\|\subset B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)\times(-\sigma_{j}/2,\sigma_{j}/2). $$

We establish some notation. To distinguish objects in $T_{x}M$ from objects in $M$ , we use lower case letters here. Let

- • $v^{j}\coloneqq(\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})_{\#}V$ ,

- • $s_{k,j}\coloneqq(\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})(\Sigma_{k})$ ,

- • $b_{\rho}\coloneqq B_{\rho}^{T_{x}M}(0)$ ,

- • $c_{\rho,\sigma}\coloneqq\partial b_{\rho}\cap\{x_{3}\in[-\sigma,\sigma]\}$ ,

- • $d_{\rho,\sigma}^{+}\coloneqq\partial b_{\rho}\cap\{x_{3}>\sigma\}$ ,

- • $d_{\rho,\sigma}^{-}\coloneqq\partial b_{\rho}\cap\{x_{3}<-\sigma\}$ .

By (10.4), we have

$$ \limsup_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(s_{k,j}\cap(B_{1}^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(0)\times([-1,1]\setminus(-\sigma_{j}/2,\sigma_{j}/2))))=0. $$

By (10.5) and the coarea formula, for almost every $\rho<1$ we have

$$ \limsup_{k}\mathcal{H}^{1}(s_{k,j}\cap(d_{\rho,\sigma_{j}/2}^{+}\cup d_{\rho,\sigma_{j}/2}^{-}))=0 $$

for every $j$ . Fix some $\rho_{1}\in(3/4,1)$ satisfying (10.6) so that $s_{k,j}$ has transverse intersection with $\partial b_{\rho_{1}}$ for every $k$ and $j$ , which is guaranteed by Sard’s theorem.

Fix some $\zeta>0$ . For $k\geq k_{1}(j,\zeta,\rho_{1})$ , we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{1}(s_{k,j}\cap(d_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{j}/2}^{+}\cup d_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{j}/2}^{-}))<\zeta. $$

For $\zeta\leq\zeta_{1}(M)$ , the coarea formula gives

$$ s_{k,j}\cap(\partial d_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}^{+}\cup\partial d_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}^{-})=\varnothing, $$

for a sequence $\sigma_{k,j}\in(\sigma_{j}/2,\sigma_{j})$ .

We apply Lemma 8.2 to $s_{k,j}\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(b_{\rho_{1}})$ with constant $\xi$ . We obtain the replacement $\tilde{s}_{k,j}\in\mathcal{D}(b_{\rho_{1}})[s_{k,j}]$ and a collection of disks $\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}$ composing $\tilde{s}_{k,j}$ in $b_{\rho_{1}}$ .

Let $\xi^{\prime}\in[\xi,2\xi]$ so that

$$ \|v^{j}\|(\partial b_{\rho_{1}-\xi^{\prime}})=0 $$

for all $j$ .

By Lemma 8.2(8.4) and (8.9) (also using (10.9)), we have

$$ v^{j}\llcorner G(b_{\rho_{1}-\xi^{\prime}},2)=\lim_{k}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}}\mathbf{v}(d\cap b_{\rho_{1}-\xi^{\prime}}). $$

Step 1: We show that we can throw away disks $d\in\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}$ with boundary in the caps $d_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}^{\pm}$ . Let $\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}$ be the set of all such disks in $\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}$ . For every $d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}$ , let $f_{d}$ be the isoperimetric region for $\partial d$ in $d_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}^{+}\cup d_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}^{-}$ . By (10.7) and Lemma 8.2(8.10), we have

$$ \sum_{d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial d)\leq\zeta $$

for $k\geq k_{1}(j,\zeta,\rho_{1})$ . By the isoperimetric inequality in the round sphere, we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(f_{d})\leq\beta_{1}\mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial d)^{2} $$

for all $d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}$ . Hence, we have

$$ \sum_{d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(f_{d})\leq\beta_{1}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial d)^{2}\leq\beta_{1}\left(\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{1}(\partial d)\right)^{2}\leq\beta_{1}\zeta^{2} $$

for $k\geq k_{1}(j,\zeta,\rho_{1})$ . Consider the competitor given by replacing each $d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}$ by $f_{d}$ (and then resolving the overlaps without increasing area by more than $\varepsilon_{k}$ by [AS79, Corollary 1]). By (10.2), Lemma 8.2(8.8), and the fact that $|d\phi_{x}|\raisebox{-1.99997pt}{$\big|_{B_{\rho/r_{j}}^{M}(x)}$}\leq 1+o_{j}(1)$ , we have

$$ r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}\setminus\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)+r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(f_{d})+2cr_{j}^{-3}\mathcal{H}^{3}(b_{\rho_{1}})+2\varepsilon_{k}+o(r_{j}^{-2}). $$

Rewriting, we have

$$ \sum_{d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq\beta_{1}\zeta^{2}+\frac{2c\mathcal{H}^{3}(b_{1})}{r_{j}}+2r_{j}^{2}\varepsilon_{k}+o_{j}(1) $$

for $k\geq k_{1}(j,\zeta,\rho_{1})$ . Taking $j\geq j_{2}(M,\xi)$ and $\zeta\leq\zeta_{2}(M,\xi)$ , and then taking $k\geq k_{2}(j,\zeta,\rho_{1},\xi)$ , we can apply Lemma 9.1 to conclude that

$$ \lim_{k}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{C}_{k,j}}\mathbf{v}(d\cap b_{\rho_{1}-\xi})=0 $$

for all $j\geq j_{2}(M,\xi)$ .

Step 2: We show that we can throw away the disks with nullhomotopic boundary in $c_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}$ . Let $\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}$ be the set of all such disks in $\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}$ . By the monotonicity of (6.5), there is a uniform upper bound for the mass of $v^{j}$ in $b_{1}$ for all $j$ depending on $V$ and $c$ .

Let $\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{-}\subset\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}$ be the set of disks $d\in\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}$ with $\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq\frac{\xi^{2}}{48\beta_{1}}$ . By the uniform mass upper bound, there is an $m=m(V,c,\xi)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that

$$ \sum_{d\in\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{-}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq m\frac{\xi^{2}}{48\beta_{1}} $$

for all $j$ . By a standard counting argument, we can partition $\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{-}$ into $2m$ disjoint sets $\{\mathfrak{N}^{-}_{k,j,i}\}_{i=1}^{2m}$ (some potentially empty) such that

$$ \sum_{d\in\mathfrak{N}^{-}_{k,j,i}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq\frac{\xi^{2}}{48\beta_{1}}. $$

By Lemma 9.1, we have

$$ \lim_{k}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{-}}\mathbf{v}(d\cap b_{\rho_{1}-\xi})=\sum_{i=1}^{2m}\lim_{k}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{N}_{k,j,i}^{-}}\mathbf{v}(d\cap b_{\rho_{1}-\xi})=0. $$

Let $\mathfrak{N}^{+}_{k,j}$ denote the set of disk $d\in\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}$ with $\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)>\frac{\xi^{2}}{48\beta_{1}}$ . By the uniform mass upper bound, we have $\#\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{+}\leq m$ . Let $f_{d}$ denote the isoperimetric region in $c_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}$ for $\partial d$ . Consider the competitor given by replacing $d$ with $f_{d}$ for all $d\in\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{+}$ (and then resolving overlaps without increasing area by more than $\varepsilon_{k}$ by [AS79, Corollary 1]). As in step 1, (10.2) and Lemma 8.2(8.8) imply

$$ r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}\setminus\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{+}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)+r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{+}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(f_{d})+2cr_{j}^{-3}\mathcal{H}^{3}(b_{\rho_{1}})+2\varepsilon_{k}+o(r_{j}^{-2}). $$

Rewriting, we have

$$ \sum_{d\in\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{+}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq m\mathcal{H}^{2}(c_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{j}})+\frac{2c\mathcal{H}^{3}(b_{1})}{r_{j}}+2r_{j}^{2}\varepsilon_{k}+o_{j}(1). $$

Assuming $j\geq j_{3}(c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ and then taking $k\geq k_{3}(j,\rho_{1},M,\xi)$ , we have $\#\mathfrak{N}_{k,j}^{+}=0$ .

Step 3: We obtain lower and upper bounds for the area of the disks whose boundary is homotopically nontrivial in $c_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}$ . Let $\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}$ denote the set of such disks in $\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}$ .

Let $d\in\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}$ . Since $\partial d$ is homotopically nontrivial in $c_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}$ , (10.5) implies

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(d\cap b_{\rho})\geq\pi(\rho-\xi)^{2} $$

for $\rho\in[\rho_{1}-2\xi,\rho_{1}]$ , $j\geq j_{4}(\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ , and $k\geq k_{4}(j,\rho_{1},M,\xi)$ .

By the uniform mass bound on the limit, there is an $m=m(c,V)$ so that $\#\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}\leq m$ for all $j\geq j_{4}(c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ and $k\geq k_{4}^{\prime}(j,c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ .

For each $d\in\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}$ , let $m_{d}$ be the disk with $\partial m_{d}=\partial d$ so that $m_{d}\setminus b_{\rho_{1}}\subset c_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}$ and $m_{d}\cap b_{\rho_{1}}$ is the flat disk $d_{k,j}^{*}\subset b_{\rho_{1}}$ with boundary $\partial d_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}}^{+}$ . Note that

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(m_{d})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(c_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j}})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(d_{k,j}^{*}). $$

Consider the competitor given by replacing each $d\in\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}$ with $m_{d}$ (and then resolving overlaps using [AS79, Corollary 1]). As in steps 1 and 2, (10.2) implies

$$ r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{S}_{k,j}\setminus\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d)+r_{j}^{-2}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(m_{d})+2cr_{j}^{-3}\mathcal{H}^{3}(b_{\rho_{1}})+2\varepsilon_{k}+o(r_{j}^{-2}). $$

Rewriting, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d) \displaystyle\leq(\#\mathfrak{L}_{k,j})(\mathcal{H}^{2}(d_{k,j}^{*})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(c_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{j}}))+\frac{2c\mathcal{H}^{3}(b_{1})}{r_{j}}+2r_{j}^{2}\varepsilon_{k}+o_{j}(1). $$

Assuming $j\geq j_{5}(c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ and then taking $k\geq k_{5}(j,c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ , we have for every $d\in\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}$ (by (10.13))

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(d)\leq\pi(\rho_{1}+\xi)^{2}. $$

Step 4: We compute the density of $V$ at $x$ . By (10.9) and the above work, we have

$$ \|v^{j}\|(b_{\rho_{1}-\xi^{\prime}})=\lim_{k}\sum_{d\in\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(d\cap b_{\rho_{1}-\xi^{\prime}}). $$

By (10.13) and (10.14), we have

$$ (\limsup_{k}\#\mathfrak{L}_{k,j})\pi(\rho_{1}-\xi)^{2}\leq\|v^{j}\|(b_{\rho_{1}-\xi^{\prime},j})\leq(\liminf_{k}\#\mathfrak{L}_{k,j})\pi(\rho_{1}+\xi)^{2}. $$

Assuming $\xi$ is sufficiently small (depending on universal quantities), we have $\lim_{k}\#\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}$ exists, so we have $\#\mathfrak{L}_{k,j}=n_{j}\in\mathbb{N}$ for all $j\geq j_{5}(c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ and $k\geq k_{6}(j,c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ . By the monotonicity of (6.5), $n_{j}$ is decreasing for $j\geq j_{6}(c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ . By Lemma 10.1, we have $n_{j}\geq 1$ . Hence, we have $n_{j}\equiv n\geq 1$ for all $j\geq j_{6}^{\prime}(c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ . Therefore, we have

$$ n-o_{\xi}(1)\leq\Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)\leq n+o_{\xi}(1). $$

Since $\xi$ is arbitrary, we conclude that $\Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)=n\in\mathbb{N}$ , i.e. $V$ has integer density at all points $x$ in its support such that some tangent cone $C\in\mathrm{VarTan}(V,x)$ is supported in a 2-plane $P_{C}\subset T_{x}M$ .

Flatness of Tangent Cones. We now show that for all $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ , every tangent cone $C\in\mathrm{VarTan}(V,x)$ is supported in some 2-plane $P_{C}\subset T_{x}M$ .

#### Lemma 10.3 (Flatness).

Let $U,\Sigma_{k},V$ be as in the statement of Theorem 10.2. If $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ and $C\in\mathrm{VarTan}(V,x)$ , then $\mathrm{spt}\|C\|\subset P_{C}$ for some 2-plane $P_{C}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ , and let $C\in\mathrm{VarTan}(V,x)$ . There is a subsequence (not relabeled) and radii $r_{k}\to\infty$ so that $v^{k}:=(\mu_{r_{k}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})_{\#}V\rightharpoonup C$ . By selecting a further subsequence (not relabeled), the surfaces $s_{k}:=(\mu_{r_{k}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})(\Sigma_{k})$ satisfy

$$ \mathbf{v}(s_{k})\rightharpoonup C. $$

We can choose the subsequence so that $r_{k}^{2}\varepsilon_{k}\to 0$ .

By Sard’s theorem, we can find a radius $r>0$ so that $b_{r}:=b_{r}^{T_{x}M}(0)$ satisfies $s_{k}\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(b_{r})$ for all $k$ . Note that by (10.2) (and the same argument as step 1 above), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(s_{k})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(s_{k}^{\prime})+r_{k}^{-1}T_{h}(s_{k},s_{k}^{\prime})+r_{k}^{2}\varepsilon_{k}+o_{k}(1) $$

for all $s_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(b_{r})[s_{k}]$ .

We apply Lemma 8.2 to $s_{k}$ in $b_{r}$ with constant $\theta<r/2$ , producing new disks $\tilde{s}_{k}$ so that

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{s}_{k})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(s_{k}^{\prime})+r_{k}^{-1}T_{h}(\tilde{s}_{k},s_{k}^{\prime})+r_{k}^{2}\varepsilon_{k}+o_{k}(1) $$

for all $s_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(b_{r})[\tilde{s}_{k}]$ . By (8.9), we have

$$ \lim_{k\to\infty}\mathbf{v}(\tilde{s}_{k}\cap b_{r/2})=C\llcorner G(b_{r/2},2). $$

Since $\tilde{s}_{k}\triangle s_{k}^{\prime}\subset b_{r}$ for all $s_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(b_{r})[\tilde{s}_{k}]$ by Lemma 8.2, we have $T_{h}(\tilde{s}_{k},s_{k}^{\prime})\leq c\mathcal{H}^{3}(b_{r})<\infty$ . Hence,

$$ \varepsilon_{k}^{\prime}\coloneqq r_{k}^{-1}T_{h}(s_{k},s_{k}^{\prime})+r_{k}^{2}\varepsilon_{k}+o_{k}(1) $$

satisfies $\varepsilon_{k}^{\prime}\to 0$ , and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{s}_{k})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(s_{k}^{\prime})+\varepsilon_{k}^{\prime} $$

for all $s_{k}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(b_{r})[\tilde{s}_{k}]$ .

Since we have shown the disks $\tilde{s}_{k}$ are a minimizing sequence for area with respect to competitors $s_{k}^{\prime}$ in the class $\mathcal{D}(b_{r})[\tilde{s}_{k}]$ , we can now conclude by following the proof strategy of [AS79].

Indeed, we observe that [AS79, Theorem 3 and Corollary 2] hold for the area minimization problem restricted to $\mathcal{D}(b_{r})[\tilde{s}_{k}]$ . Case I and Case II in the proof of [AS79, Theorem 3] follow directly from the argument in [AS79]. As for Case III, note that the relevant step in the proof only uses disks obtained from the replacement procedure (which lie in our restricted set of competitors) and comparison to isoperimetric regions (also in the restricted set of competitors). The rest of the proofs are unchanged. ∎

Lemma 10.3, together with the previous step of the proof, shows that $V$ has positive integer density at every point of its support.

Decomposition of $V$ . To study the local regularity of $V$ , we return to work in $M$ . We adapt the set up from the proof of integer density. Let $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ , $\xi>0$ , $r_{j}\to\infty$ , $\sigma_{j}\to 0$ , $\zeta>0$ , $\sigma_{k,j}\in(\sigma_{j}/2,\sigma_{j})$ as above. We define

- • $B_{\rho,j}:=B_{\rho/r_{j}}^{M}(x)$ ,

- • $C_{\rho,\sigma,j}:=(\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})^{-1}(c_{\rho,\sigma})\subset B_{\rho,j}$ ,

- • $D_{\rho,\sigma,j}^{\pm}:=(\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})^{-1}(d_{\rho,\sigma}^{\pm})\subset B_{\rho,j}$ .

We apply Lemma 8.2 to $\Sigma_{k}\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(B_{\rho_{1},j})$ with constant $\xi$ , producing new disks $S_{k,j}$ . By (8.5), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(S_{k,j})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(S_{k,j}^{\prime})+T_{h}(S_{k,j},S_{k,j}^{\prime})+\varepsilon_{k} $$

for all $S_{k,j}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(B_{\rho_{1},j})[S_{k,j}]$ . Let $\mathcal{S}_{k,j}$ be the set of disks composing $S_{k,j}$ in $B_{\rho_{1},j}$ . Let $\mathcal{L}_{k,j}\subset\mathcal{S}_{k,j}$ be the disks with homotopically nontrivial boundary in $C_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j},j}$ . We translate the estimates from the proof of integer density to $M$ .

Henceforth we assume $j\geq j_{6}^{\prime}(c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ and $k\geq k_{6}(j,c,\rho_{1},M,V,\xi)$ as above. Namely, we have $\#\mathcal{L}_{k,j}=n$ for all such $j$ and $k$ .

Label the disks $D\in\mathcal{L}_{k,j}$ as $\{D_{k,j,1},\ldots,D_{k,j,n}\}$ . There is a subsequence (not relabeled, after shuffling the 1 through $n$ labels) so that $\mathbf{v}(D_{k,j,i})$ converges in the varifold sense to a limit $V_{j,i}$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$ as $k\to\infty$ , satisfying

$$ \|V_{j,i}\|(B_{\rho_{1}-2\xi,j})\geq\pi(\rho_{1}-4\xi)^{2}r_{j}^{-2}\ \ \text{and}\ \ \|V_{j,i}\|(B_{\rho_{1},j})\leq\pi(\rho_{1}+2\xi)^{2}r_{j}^{-2}, $$

$$ \mathrm{spt}\|V_{j,i}\|\subset(\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})^{-1}(B_{\rho_{1}}^{T_{x}M}(0)\cap\{-\sigma_{j}\leq x_{3}\leq\sigma_{j}\}), $$

and

$$ V\llcorner G(B_{\rho_{1}-2\xi,j},2)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}V_{j,i}\llcorner G(B_{\rho_{1}-2\xi,j},2). $$

Reduction to Stacked Disk Minimization. We now reduce the problem to a stacked disk minimization problem.

Let $\mathcal{E}_{k,j}\coloneqq\mathcal{S}_{k,j}\setminus\mathcal{L}_{k,j}$ . For $D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}$ let $F_{D}\subset\partial B_{\rho_{1},j}$ be the isoperimetric region for $\partial D$ . Let $\Lambda_{D}\subset B_{\rho_{1},j}$ be the open set bounded by $D\cup F_{D}$ .

Steps 1 and 2 from the proof of integer density above imply

$$ \limsup_{k}\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D\cap B_{1/2,j})=0. $$

In particular, (10.11) and (10.12) imply

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{D})\leq A(\xi,\zeta,j,k) $$

with $A(\xi,\zeta,j,k)\to 0$ as $(\xi,\zeta)\to 0$ and $j,k\to\infty$ . By (8.2), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(\Lambda_{D})\leq c_{1}A(\xi,\zeta,j,k)^{3/2}. $$

Taking $\xi$ and $\zeta$ small and $j$ and $k$ large, the coarea formula implies

$$ \limsup_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Lambda_{D}\cap\partial B_{\rho,j})\leq\frac{1}{4}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B_{1/4,j})\leq\frac{1}{4}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\partial B_{\rho,j}) $$

for $\rho$ in a set of positive measure in $(1/4,1/2)$ . By the coarea formula and (10.20), we have

$$ \limsup_{k}\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{1}(D\cap\partial B_{\rho,j})=0 $$

for almost every $\rho\in(1/4,1/2)$ . Take $\rho\in(1/4,1/2)$ satisfying (10.22) and (10.23). By the coarea formula and (10.23), we have

$$ \limsup_{k}\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{0}(D\cap\partial C_{\rho,\sigma,j})=0 $$

for $\sigma$ in a set of positive measure in $(\sigma_{0}/4,\sigma_{0}/2)$ .

For $D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}$ , let $B_{D}$ be the unique component of $D\setminus B_{\rho,j}$ containing $\partial D$ . Note that $B_{D}$ is a punctured disk with boundary $\partial D\cup\bigcup_{l}\alpha_{l}$ , where $\alpha_{l}$ are smooth Jordan curves in $\partial B_{\rho,j}$ . Let $N_{D}$ be a smooth disk in $\overline{B}_{\rho_{1},j}\setminus\overline{B}_{\rho,j}$ obtained by gluing $F_{\alpha_{l}}$ (the isoperimetric region in $\partial B_{\rho,j}$ for $\alpha_{l}$ ) to $B_{D}$ and then smoothing. This procedure is well-defined as long as $F_{\alpha_{l}}$ is glued and perturbed before $F_{\alpha_{l^{\prime}}}$ if $F_{\alpha_{l}}\subset F_{\alpha_{l^{\prime}}}$ . Moreover, the resulting surface is a disk by construction.

We construct a competitor $\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\in\mathcal{D}(B_{\rho_{1},j})[S_{k,j}]$ by replacing each $D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}$ by $N_{D}$ . Since the surfaces $B_{D}$ are disjoint, we can choose the smoothing so that the surfaces $N_{D}$ are also disjoint, so $\mathbf{S}_{k,j}$ is well-defined.

We claim that we can replace $S_{k,j}$ by $\mathbf{S}_{k,j}$ in (10.16) after replacing $\varepsilon_{k}$ by some $\varepsilon_{k,j}$ satisfying $\lim_{k}\varepsilon_{k,j}=0$ . Note that $N_{D}$ is obtained from $D$ by (a) applying Lemma 4.3 to each component of $D\setminus B_{\rho,j}$ except $B_{D}$ , (b) deleting everything in $\overline{B}_{\rho,j}$ , and (c) turning $B_{D}$ into $N_{D}$ as described above. By Lemma 4.3 and (10.21), the $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ functional does not increase after (a). Since we only delete portions of the surface in (b), the area does not increase from (b). By (8.2), (4.5), and (10.22), we have (for $k$ large)

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Lambda_{D}\cap B_{\rho,j}) \displaystyle\leq c_{1}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D\cap B_{\rho,j})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Lambda_{D}\cap\partial B_{\rho,j}))^{3/2} \displaystyle\leq c_{1}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D\cap B_{\rho,j})+\beta_{0}\mathcal{H}^{1}(D\cap\partial B_{\rho,j})^{2})^{3/2} $$

Hence, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}} \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Lambda_{D}\cap B_{\rho,j})\leq c_{1}\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D\cap B_{\rho,j})+\beta_{0}\mathcal{H}^{1}(D\cap\partial B_{\rho,j})^{2})^{3/2} \displaystyle\leq c_{1}\left(\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D\cap B_{\rho,j})+\beta_{0}\mathcal{H}^{1}(D\cap\partial B_{\rho,j})^{2})\right)^{3/2} \displaystyle\leq c_{1}\left(\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D\cap B_{\rho,j})+\beta_{0}\left(\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{1}(D\cap\partial B_{\rho,j})\right)^{2}\right)^{3/2} $$

and the right hand side goes to zero by (10.20) and (10.23). Therefore the volume change from (b) vanishes as $k\to\infty$ . Finally, by (10.23) and (4.5), we have $\lim_{k}\sum_{\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(N_{D}\triangle B_{D})=0$ , so the area added in (c) vanishes as $k\to\infty$ . Hence, we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\mathbf{S}_{k,j})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(S_{k,j}^{\prime})+T_{h}(\mathbf{S}_{k,j},S_{k,j}^{\prime})+\varepsilon_{k,j} $$

for all $S_{k,j}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(B_{\rho_{1},j})[\mathbf{S}_{k,j}]$ , where $\lim_{k}\varepsilon_{k,j}=0$ .

Let $D_{k,j,i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(B_{\rho,j})[D_{k,j,i}]$ be mutually disjoint for $i=1,\ldots,n$ . Let $\Omega_{k,j,i}$ be the open set in $B_{\rho_{1},j}$ so that

$$ \partial[\Omega_{k,j,i}]\llcorner B_{\rho_{1},j}=[D_{k,j,i}]\llcorner B_{\rho_{1},j}. $$

Let $\Omega_{k,j,i}^{\prime}$ be the analogous open set for $D_{k,j,i}^{\prime}$ . We claim that

$$ \sum_{i}\left(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,i})-\int_{\Omega_{k,j,i}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\right)\leq\sum_{i}\left(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,i}^{\prime})-\int_{\Omega_{k,j,i}^{\prime}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\right)+\varepsilon_{k,j}^{\prime\prime} $$

for some $\lim_{k}\varepsilon_{k,j}^{\prime\prime}\to 0$ .

Consider the competitor $S_{k,j}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(B_{\rho_{1},j})[\mathbf{S}_{k,j}]$ given by replacing each $D_{k,j,i}$ by $D_{k,j,i}^{\prime}$ . This competitor is well-defined (i.e. there are no self-intersections) because $(\mathbf{S}_{k,j}\setminus\bigcup_{i}D_{k,j,i})\cap B_{\rho,j}=\varnothing$ by definition, and $D_{k,j,i}^{\prime}\setminus\overline{B}_{\rho,j}$ is a subset of $D_{k,j,i}$ . Hence, (10.27) follows directly from (10.26).

We conclude with some notation. Let $B_{k,j,i}$ be the open set in $B_{\rho_{1},j}$ so that

$$ \partial B_{k,j,i}\setminus D_{k,j,i}\subset\partial B_{\rho_{1},j}\ \ \text{and}\ \ D_{\rho_{1},\sigma_{k,j},j}^{-}\subset\partial B_{k,j,i}. $$

If $B_{k,j,i}\subset B_{k,j,i^{\prime}}$ for some $i\neq i^{\prime}$ , then we say $D_{k,j,i}<D_{k,j,i^{\prime}}$ . If $B_{k,j,i}=\Omega_{k,j,i}$ (as defined above), then we say $D_{k,j,i}$ is oriented up; otherwise, it is oriented down. By selecting a subsequence and relabeling, we can assume that

$$ D_{k,j,1}>D_{k,j,2}>\ldots>D_{k,j,n}, $$

and that $D_{k,j,i}$ is oriented up if and only if $D_{k^{\prime},j,i}$ is oriented up for all $k^{\prime}\neq k$ . By the assumption that there is an open set $\Lambda_{k}$ with $\partial\Lambda_{k}\cap U=\Sigma_{k}\cap U$ , we conclude that $D_{k,j,i}$ is oriented up if and only if $D_{k,j,i-1}$ and $D_{k,j,i+1}$ are oriented down (i.e. the orientation alternates with respect to the order of the disks).

Parity for Stacked Disks. Let $\Omega_{k}$ and $\Omega$ be defined as in Theorem 6.1 with respect to the set $U$ . Let $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ . We claim that

$$ \Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)\equiv 0\mod 2\implies x\notin\partial^{*}\Omega, $$

and

$$ \Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)\equiv 1\mod 2\implies x\in\overline{\partial^{*}\Omega}. $$

Let $W$ be any neighborhood of $x$ . Taking $j$ large enough, we have $B_{\rho_{1},j}\subset W$ . Let $\Omega_{k,j,i}$ be defined as above for the stacked disks $D_{k,j,i}$ . Let $\Omega_{k,j}$ be the open subset of $B_{\rho_{1},j}$ satisfying

$$ \partial[\Omega_{k,j}]\llcorner B_{\rho_{1},j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}[D_{k,j,i}]\llcorner B_{\rho_{1},j}. $$

Let $\Omega^{j,i}$ and $\Omega^{j}$ be the limits of $\Omega_{k,j,i}$ and $\Omega_{k,j}$ in $k$ respectively, in the sense of Theorem 6.1.

We first show that $\mathcal{H}^{3}((\Omega^{j}\triangle\Omega))\cap B_{\rho,j})=0$ . Indeed, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{3}((\Omega^{j}\triangle\Omega)\cap B_{\rho,j}) \displaystyle=\lim_{k}\mathcal{H}^{3}((\Omega_{k,j}\triangle\Omega_{k})\cap B_{\rho,j}) \displaystyle\leq\lim_{k}\mathcal{H}^{3}(\beta_{k})+\sum_{D\in\mathcal{E}_{k,j}}\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Lambda_{D}\cap B_{\rho,j})=0, $$

by Lemma 8.2(8.9) and (10.25) (where $\beta_{k}$ are the bubbles called “ $B$ ” in Lemma 8.2). Hence, we have

$$ \partial^{*}\Omega\cap B_{\rho,j}=\partial^{*}\Omega^{j}\cap B_{\rho,j}, $$

so it suffices to work with $\Omega^{j}$ .

Let $\omega^{j}:=(\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})(\Omega^{j})$ . Let $v_{j,i}:=(\mu_{r_{j}}\circ\phi_{x}^{-1})_{\#}V_{j,i}$ . By (10.18), we have

$$ \mathrm{spt}\left\|\sum_{i}v_{j,i}\right\|\cap b_{\rho}\subset b_{\rho}\cap\{-\sigma_{j}\leq x_{3}\leq\sigma_{j}\}. $$

Let

$$ b_{\rho,j}^{+}\coloneqq b_{\rho}\cap\{x_{3}>\sigma_{j}\}\ \ \text{and}\ \ b_{\rho,j}^{-}\coloneqq b_{\rho}\cap\{x_{3}<-\sigma_{j}\}. $$

Since $\overline{\partial^{*}\omega^{j}}\cap b_{\rho}\subset\mathrm{spt}\|\sum_{i}v_{j,i}\|\cap b_{\rho}$ , we have either $b_{\rho,j}^{+}\subset\omega^{j}$ or $b_{\rho,j}^{+}\cap\omega^{j}=\varnothing$ (and analogously for $b_{\rho,j}^{-}$ ). We see that $D_{k,j,1}$ is oriented down if and only if $b_{\rho,j}^{+}\subset\omega^{j}$ . Similarly, $D_{k,j,n}$ is oriented up if and only if $b_{\rho,j}^{-}\subset\omega^{j}$ . Note that $b_{\rho,j}^{\pm}$ contain a definite portion of $b_{2}^{\pm}$ (the upper and lower half balls of radius 2 in $T_{x}M$ ).

If $n\equiv 1\mod 2$ , then $\omega^{j}$ converges in $L^{1}$ as $j\to\infty$ (without loss of generality) to the upper half space $H^{+}\subset T_{x}M$ . Hence, every sufficiently small neighborhood $W$ of $x$ satisfies

$$ 0<\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega\cap W)<\mathcal{H}^{3}(W), $$

so we have $x\in\overline{\partial^{*}\Omega}$ .

If $n\equiv 0\mod 2$ , then $\omega^{j}$ converges in $L^{1}$ as $j\to\infty$ to $T_{x}M$ or $\varnothing$ , so $x\notin\partial^{*}\Omega$ (i.e. we showed $x$ is not in the essential boundary of $\Omega$ , which contains the reduced boundary (see [Mag12, Theorem 16.2]).

$C^{1,\alpha}$ Regularity. By Lemma 7.7(7.10) and (10.27), we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,i})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,i}^{\prime})+c|T(D_{k,j,i},D_{k,j,i^{\prime}})|+\varepsilon_{k,j} $$

for any $D_{k,j,i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(B_{\rho,j})[D_{k,j,i}]$ .

We observe that everything we have proved thus far only requires that the function $h$ is measurable and satisfies $|h|\leq c$ . We note that (10.30) implies that $D_{k,j,i}$ is a minimizing sequence for the problem with prescribing function $-c+2c\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{j,i}}$ . Hence, all of the above work applies to $V_{j,i}$ . In particular, $V_{j,i}$ has $c$ -bounded first variation and positive integer density in its support. By (10.17), there is a neighborhood $W$ of $x$ so that $\Theta^{2}(V_{j,i},y)=1$ for all $y\in W\cap\mathrm{spt}\|V_{j,i}\|$ .

By [All72, §8], we have $V_{j,i}\llcorner G(W,2)=\mathbf{v}(N_{j,i},1)$ for a $C^{1.\alpha}$ surface $N_{j,i}\subset W$ . By (10.29), we have $N_{j,i}\cap W=\partial^{*}\Omega^{j,i}\cap W$ . Hence, $N_{j,i}$ is on one side of $N_{j,i^{\prime}}$ for any $i,\ i^{\prime}$ , and each of these surfaces intersects tangentially at $x$ . We conclude by (10.19).

Decomposition into 1-Stacks and 2-Stacks. Take $x$ so that $h(x)\neq 0$ . Suppose without loss of generality (by swapping orientations and taking $j$ sufficiently large) that $h|_{B_{\rho_{1},j}}>0$ . We now decompose the stacked disk minimization problem (10.27) into smaller units, which we call 1-stacks and 2-stacks.

We first separate the 1-stacks. If $D_{k,j,1}$ is oriented up, then we show that

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,1})-\int_{\Omega_{k,j,1}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,1}^{\prime})-\int_{\Omega_{k,j,1}^{\prime}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}+\varepsilon_{k,j} $$

for all $D_{k,j,1}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(B_{\rho,j})[D_{k,j,1}]$ , where $\Omega_{k,j,1}^{\prime}$ is defined as above. The analogous statement holds if $D_{k,j,n}$ is oriented down by vertical reflection. The result follows immediately from Lemma 7.8.

Now we separate the 2-stacks. If $D_{k,j,i^{\prime}}$ is oriented down for some $1\leq i^{\prime}<n$ , then we show that

$$ \sum_{i=i^{\prime}}^{i^{\prime}+1}\left(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,i})-\int_{\Omega_{k,j,i}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\right)\leq\sum_{i=i^{\prime}}^{i^{\prime}+1}\left(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,i}^{\prime})-\int_{\Omega_{k,j,i}^{\prime}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\right)+\varepsilon_{k}^{\prime} $$

for all mutually disjoint $D_{k,j,i}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(B_{\rho,j})[D_{k,j,i}]$ for $i=i^{\prime},\ i^{\prime}+1$ , where $\Omega_{k,j,i}^{\prime}$ is defined as above. The result follows immediately from Lemma 7.9.

Regularity of 1-Stacks. Suppose (10.31) holds88 8 We note that (10.31) holds at any point in $V$ of density 1, as well as in the case $D_{k,j,1}$ is oriented up.. Recall that we showed $\Theta^{2}(V_{j,1},y)=1$ for all $y\in W\cap\mathrm{spt}\|V_{j,1}\|$ and

$$ \mathrm{spt}\|V_{j,1}\|\cap W=\partial^{*}\Omega^{j,1}\cap W. $$

Hence, we have

$$ \|V_{j,1}\|\llcorner W=|D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega^{j,1}}|\llcorner W. $$

Inserting this equality into Theorem 6.1(6.3), we conclude that

$$ H_{V_{j,1}}|_{W}=h\nu_{\partial^{*}\Omega^{j,1}}|_{W}, $$

which is a $C^{1,\alpha}$ vector field. Applying the regularity theorem of Allard [All72, §8] iteratively, we conclude that $N_{j,1}$ is a smooth surface with prescribed mean curvature $h$ in $W$ with respect to the set $\Omega^{j,1}$ . Stability follows from smooth embeddedness and (6.2).

Regularity of 2-Stacks. Suppose $D_{k,j,i^{\prime}}$ is oriented down for $1\leq i^{\prime}<n$ , so (10.32) holds. For ease of notation, let $i^{\prime}=1$ .

We show the mean convexity of $V_{j,1}$ . Let $X$ be a smooth vector field with compact support in $B_{\rho,j}$ , and let $\Phi_{t}$ be the flow of $X$ . Without loss of generality, we suppose that

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\|(\Phi_{t})_{\#}V_{1}\|(B_{\rho,j})<0, $$

(i.e. either the derivative is zero, or we can swap $X\mapsto-X$ ). By Lemma 7.7(7.11) and (10.32), we have (using $h\geq 0$ )

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k,j,1}\cap B_{\rho,j})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Phi_{t}(D_{k,j,1})\cap B_{\rho,j})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega_{k,j,1}\setminus\Phi_{t}(\Omega_{k,j,1}))+\varepsilon_{k}^{\prime\prime}. $$

Following the proof of Theorem 6.1, we have

$$ \|V_{j,1}\|(B_{\rho,j})\leq\|(\Phi_{t})_{\#}V_{j,1}\|(B_{\rho,j})+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{j,1}\setminus\Phi_{t}(\Omega^{j,1})). $$

Hence, we have

$$ 0>\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\|(\Phi_{t})_{\#}V_{j,1}\|(B_{\rho,j})\geq-c\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0^{+}}\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{j,1}\setminus\Phi_{t}(\Omega^{j,1})). $$

By [Mag12, Proposition 17.8], we have

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0^{+}}\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{j,1}\setminus\Phi_{t}(\Omega^{j,1}))\leq\int_{\partial^{*}\Omega_{1}}(X\cdot\nu_{\partial^{*}\Omega^{j,1}})_{-}\ d\mathcal{H}^{2}. $$

Hence, we observe that the first variation cannot be negative if $X\cdot\nu_{\partial^{*}\Omega^{j,1}}\geq 0$ , which proves the desired weak mean convexity. By vertical reflection, the same holds for $V_{j,2}$ .

Suppose $\mathrm{spt}\|V_{j,1}\|\cap W^{\prime}=\mathrm{spt}\|V_{j,2}\|\cap W^{\prime}$ for some open set $W^{\prime}\subset W$ . As shown above, $\Theta^{2}(V_{j,1}+V_{j,2},x)=2$ for all $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V_{j,1}+V_{j,2}\|\cap W^{\prime}$ . By (10.28), we have $\partial^{*}(\Omega^{j,1}\cup\Omega^{j,2})\cap W^{\prime}=\varnothing$ , so in fact $\overline{\partial^{*}(\Omega^{j,1}\cup\Omega^{j,2})}\cap W^{\prime}=\varnothing$ . Since we already showed $\mathrm{spt}\|V_{j,i}\|\cap W^{\prime}=\partial^{*}\Omega^{j,i}\cap W^{\prime}$ , we conclude that $\mathcal{H}^{3}((\Omega^{j,1}\cup\Omega^{j,2})\cap W^{\prime})=\mathcal{H}^{3}(W^{\prime})$ . By Theorem 6.1(6.2), $V_{j,1}+V_{j,2}$ is stationary in $W^{\prime}$ . Then by Allard’s regularity theorem [All72, §8],

$$ (V_{j,1}+V_{j,2})\llcorner G(W^{\prime},2)\cap\mathbf{v}(N,2), $$

where $N\subset W^{\prime}$ is a smooth minimal surface. Hence, $N_{j,1}\cap W^{\prime}=N_{j,2}\cap W^{\prime}=N$ . Stability follows from smooth embeddedness and Theorem 6.1(6.2).

Maximum Principle. First, suppose $\Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)=2n+1$ . Then (without loss of generality) $D_{k,j,1}$ is oriented up. By the regularity of 1-stacks, $V_{j,1}$ is the varifold associated to a smooth surface $N_{j,1}$ with mean curvature $h>0$ pointing up. Suppose for contradiction that $n\geq 1$ . Then $V_{j,2}$ is the varifold associated to a $C^{1,\alpha}$ surface $N_{j,2}$ with generalized mean curvature pointing down. Moreover, $N_{j,2}$ is below $N_{j,1}$ and intersects $N_{j,1}$ tangentially at $x$ , which contradicts the strong maximum principle (see Lemma A.2). Hence, if $D_{k,j,1}$ is oriented up, then $n=1$ and $V$ is the varifold of a smooth surface of prescribed mean curvature $h$ pointing up in a neighborhood of $x$ .

Second, suppose $\Theta^{2}(\|V\|,x)=2n$ with $n\geq 2$ . By the above paragraph, $V$ consists of $n$ 2-stacks intersecting tangentially and on one side at $x$ . Then $N_{j,2}$ and $N_{j,2n-1}$ are $C^{1,\alpha}$ surfaces on one side of each other, intersecting tangentially at $x$ , and with generalized mean curvature pointing away from each other. By the strong maximum principle (see Lemma A.2) and the regularity of 2-stacks, there is a neighborhood $W^{\prime\prime}$ of $x$ and a minimal surface $N\subset W^{\prime\prime}$ satisfying $N_{j,i}\cap W^{\prime\prime}=N$ for all $i$ . Hence, $\Theta^{2}(\|V\|,y)=2n$ for all $y\in W^{\prime\prime}\cap\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ . ∎

### 11. Improvement from Free Boundary Problems

In this section, we use some results from the theory of free boundary problems–in particular, the recent result of [WZ23b]–to obtain the optimal regularity of the limit surfaces in Theorem 10.2.

For the remainder of this section, let $V$ be as in Theorem 10.2, and $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ . Also, let $W_{x}$ be the open neighborhood of $x$ provided by Theorem 10.2, and let $N_{1},N_{2},\dots,N_{n_{x}}$ be the corresponding $C^{1,\alpha}$ surfaces meeting tangentially at $x$ .

The main result of this section is the following.

#### Proposition 11.1.

The surfaces $N_{1},\dots,N_{n_{x}}$ are $C^{1,1}$ in the interior of $W_{x}$ .

#### Proof.

We shall follow the setup in [WZ23b, §1.2].

By Theorem 10.2, $V\llcorner G(W_{x},2)=\sum_{l=1}^{n_{x}}\mathbf{v}(N_{l},1)$ , where $N_{i}$ are distinct $C^{1,\alpha}$ hypersurfaces with $\|h\|_{L^{\infty}(W_{x})}$ -bounded generalized mean curvature, such that each $N_{l}$ is on one side of $N_{l^{\prime}}$ intersecting tangentially at $x$ . Let then $n\coloneqq n_{x}$ , and let $P\subset T_{x}M$ be the common tangent plane of $N_{1},N_{2},\dots,N_{n}$ at $x$ .

By shrinking $W_{x}$ if necessary, we can assume the surfaces $N_{i}$ can be represented as weakly ordered graphs over the ball $B^{P}_{r}(0)\subset P$ for some small enough $r>0$ . By Allard’s regularity theorem (see the proof of Theorem 10.2), these graphs satisfy a uniform $C^{1,\alpha}$ bound.

By [WZ23b, Remark 1.5], after shrinking $W_{x}$ again if necessary, there is an embedded minimal surface $\Gamma\subset W_{x}$ through $x$ with boundary in $\partial W_{x}$ , so that we can rewrite $N_{1},N_{2},\dots,N_{n}$ as weakly ordered normal graphs over $\mathcal{B}_{r^{\prime}}(x)\subset\Gamma$ with uniformly bounded $C^{1,\alpha}$ norm, where $\mathcal{B}_{r^{\prime}}(x)$ denotes the geodesic ball in $\Gamma$ with center $x$ and radius $r^{\prime}$ . In particular, after choosing a unit normal field on $\Gamma$ , which trivializes the normal bundle $N\Gamma$ , there are $C^{1,\alpha}$ functions $u_{i}:\mathcal{B}_{r^{\prime}}(x)\to\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$ u_{1}\leq u_{2}\leq\dots\leq u_{n}, $$

and

$$ N_{i}=\mathrm{graph}\,u_{i} $$

for $i=1,\dots,n$ .

Notice that, when restricted to $W_{x}$ , the varifold $V$ is induced by the union of graphs of the functions $u_{i}$ , and the Caccioppoli set $\Omega$ has boundary given by $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(-1)^{i-1}[\mathrm{graph}\,u_{i}]$ in the sense of currents. By the proof of Theorem 10.2, the pair $(V,\Omega)$ is $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ -stationary in $W_{x}$ in the sense of [WZ23b].

Therefore, the first conclusion in [WZ23b, Theorem 1.4] applies, and this ends the proof of the proposition. ∎

As mentioned in the Introduction, for the curvature estimates in §17 we are going to need a $C^{1,1}$ estimate for the functions $u_{1},\dots,u_{n}$ . This also follows from [WZ23b, Theorem 1.4], after a simple rescaling. Indeed, after rescaling the metric in $W_{x}$ by a constant factor, we can assume the rescaled graph functions $\tilde{u}_{i}$ are defined on the ball $\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{2}(x)$ of radius 2, where for the rest of this section we shall use a tilde to denote quantities and balls with respect to the rescaled metric. Similarly, the prescribing function must be rescaled appropriately, so that the corresponding pair $(\tilde{V},\tilde{\Omega})$ is $\mathcal{A}^{\tilde{h}}$ -stationary. By these rescalings, we can assume that

$$ \|\tilde{u}_{i}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{2}(x))}<1 $$

for all $i=1,\dots,n$ , and

$$ \|\tilde{h}\|_{C^{1}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1}(x)\times(-1,1))}<1, $$

where $\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1}(x)\times(-1,1))$ denotes the width 1 tubular neighborhood of $\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1}(x)$ in Fermi coordinates with respect to $\Gamma$ in the rescaled metric. Again, by Theorem 10.2 each graph has $\|\tilde{h}\|_{L^{\infty}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1}(x)\times(-1,1))}$ -bounded first variation. Therefore, the second conclusion of [WZ23b, Theorem 1.4] applies, and we obtain the following $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ estimate:

#### Corollary 11.2.

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\tilde{u}_{i}\|_{C^{1,1}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1/2}(x))}\leq C\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\tilde{u}_{i}\|_{C^{1,\alpha}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1}(x)}+\|\tilde{h}\|_{C^{1}(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}_{1}(x)\times(-1,1))}\right) $$

for some constant $C\geq 1$ depending only on $n,\alpha$ , and the metric $g$ in $W_{x}$ .

Naturally, this implies a $C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{1,1}$ -estimate for the original functions $u_{i}$ .

If $h(x)\neq 0$ , we can prove a more precise regularity result. By Theorem 10.2, if $h(x)\neq 0$ , then $n_{x}\in\{1\}\cup 2\mathbb{N}$ and

- • if $n_{x}=1$ , then $V\llcorner G(W_{x},2)=\mathbf{v}(N,1)$ , where $N\subset W_{x}$ is a smooth stable surface with prescribed mean curvature $h$ ;

- • if $n_{y}=2n$ for all $y\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|\cap W_{x}^{\prime}$ for an open set $W_{x}^{\prime}\subset W_{x}$ containing $x$ , then $V\llcorner G(W^{\prime}_{x},2)=\mathbf{v}(N,2n)$ , where $N\subset W_{x}^{\prime}$ is a smooth stable minimal surface.

Hence, in both cases, the support of $V$ in a neighbourhood of $x$ coincides with a smooth surface.

We now deal with the case where $n_{x}=2n$ , and there is a sequence $x_{j}\to x$ with $x_{j}\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ and $n_{x_{j}}\neq 2n$ . By Theorem 10.2, then $n=1$ and the surfaces $N_{1},N_{2}\subset W_{x}$ intersect tangentially at $x$ . Let $T$ denote the touching set $T=N_{1}\cap N_{2}\subset W_{x}$ and let $\Gamma$ be its boundary $\partial T\cap W_{x}$ in $W_{x}$ .

#### Proposition 11.3.

The boundary $\Gamma$ of the touching set $T$ is locally contained in a $C^{1,\alpha}$ curve and satisfies $\mathcal{H}^{1}(\Gamma)<+\infty$
