## Part II Minimization over isotopy classes

In this part we follow the arguments of [MSY82], [CDL03], and [DLP10], upgrading from the regularity of minimizers of disks to the regularity of minimizers over isotopy classes.

### 12. Minimization Problem

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth $3$ -dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $h:M\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth real valued function, and let $c\coloneqq\sup_{M}|h|$ .

As before, by rescaling $M$ , we can assume that the conditions of §4.1 hold with $\rho_{0}=1$ .

Let $U\subset M$ be an open set with $C^{1}$ boundary.

Let $\mathcal{O}(U)$ be the set of open sets $\Omega\subset M$ with smooth boundary so that $\partial\Omega$ has transverse (or empty) intersection with $U$ .

In this part, we consider the following question.

#### Question 12.1.

Consider a sequence $\{\Omega_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{O}(U)$ and $\Sigma_{k}:=\partial\Omega_{k}\cap U$ satisfying $\sup_{k}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k})<\infty$ , $\sup_{k}\mathrm{genus}(\Sigma_{k})<\infty$ , and

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega_{k})\leq\mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(1,\Omega_{k}))+\varepsilon_{k} $$

for all $\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ with $\varepsilon_{k}\to 0$ . Does (a subsequence of) $\Sigma_{k}:=\partial\Omega_{j}\cap U$ converge to a regular limit with prescribed mean curvature $h$ ?

We first observe that all of the conclusions of Theorem 6.1 hold, where $\mathbf{v}(\Sigma_{k})\rightharpoonup V$ and $\Omega_{k}\cap U\to\Omega$ , by following the same proof.

### 13. Gamma-Reduction

The key insight of [MSY82] is the introduction of a procedure, called $\gamma$ -reduction, to cut away small necks that either create genus or separate large components. This procedure enables the reduction of the full isotopy minimization problem to the disk minimization problem, solved in Part I above.

#### 13.1. Definition of gamma-reduction

Let $\delta>0$ be the constant from Lemma 4.2, and let $0<\gamma<\delta^{2}/9$ . Let $U\subset M$ be an open set, and let $\Sigma\subset U$ be a smooth embedded oriented surface with $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial U$ . Let $\mathcal{C}(\Sigma,U)$ be the set of smooth embedded oriented surfaces $\Sigma^{\prime}\subset U$ with $\partial[\Sigma^{\prime}]=\partial[\Sigma]$ .

#### Definition 13.1.

For $\Sigma_{1},\ \Sigma_{2}\in\mathcal{C}(\Sigma,U)$ , we write

$$ \Sigma_{2}\overset{(\gamma,U)}{\ll}\Sigma_{1} $$

and say $\Sigma_{2}$ is a $\gamma$ -reduction of $\Sigma_{1}$ if the following hold:

- (1) $\Sigma_{2}$ is obtained from $\Sigma_{1}$ by surgery in $U$ ; namely, • $\overline{\Sigma_{1}\setminus\Sigma_{2}}=:A$ is diffeomorphic to the standard closed annulus, • $\overline{\Sigma_{2}\setminus\Sigma_{1}}=:D_{1}\cup D_{2}$ is diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of two standard closed disks, • there is an open set $Y\subset U$ homeomorphic to the standard 3-ball with $\partial Y=A\cup D_{1}\cup D_{2}$ and $Y\cap(\Sigma_{1}\cup\Sigma_{2})=\varnothing$ .

- (2) $\mathcal{H}^{2}(A)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{1})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{2})<2\gamma$ .

- (3) If $\Gamma$ is the connected component of $\Sigma_{1}$ containing $A$ , then for each component of $\Gamma\setminus A$ we have either • it is a disk of area at least $\delta^{2}/2$ , • it is not simply connected.

#### Definition 13.2.

For $\Sigma_{1},\ \Sigma_{2}\in\mathcal{C}(\Sigma,U)$ , we write

$$ \Sigma_{2}\overset{(\gamma,U)}{<}\Sigma_{1} $$

and say $\Sigma_{2}$ is a strong $\gamma$ -reduction of $\Sigma_{1}$ , if there is an isotopy $\psi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ satisfying

- (1) $\Sigma_{2}\overset{(\gamma,U)}{\ll}\psi(1,\Sigma_{1})$ ,

- (2) $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\psi(1,\Sigma_{1})\triangle\Sigma_{1})<\gamma$ .

We say a surface is $(\gamma,U)$ -irreducible (resp. strongly $(\gamma,U)$ -irreducible) if it admits no $(\gamma,U)$ reduction (resp. strong $(\gamma,U)$ -reduction).

#### 13.2. Structure of gamma-irreducible surfaces

We adapt [MSY82, Theorem 2] to our setting, allowing us to decompose $\gamma$ -irreducible surfaces in small balls into a disjoint union of disks.

#### Theorem 13.3.

Suppose $\mathcal{H}^{3}(U)\leq\eta/8$ . Let $U^{\prime}\subset\subset U$ be an open set so that $\overline{U}^{\prime}$ is diffeomorphic to $\overline{\mathbb{B}}$ . Suppose $\Omega\subset M$ satisfies

- •

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega)-\inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(1,\Omega))=:E(\Omega)\leq 3\gamma/16. $$

- • $\Sigma\coloneqq\partial\Omega\cap U$ is strongly $(\gamma,U)$ -irreducible,

- • $\Sigma$ has transverse intersection with $\partial U^{\prime}$ .

Let $\Gamma_{1},\ldots,\Gamma_{q}$ be the components of $\Sigma\cap\partial U^{\prime}$ , and let $F_{j}$ denote the isoperimetric region in $\partial U^{\prime}$ with boundary $\Gamma_{j}$ . Suppose further that

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})\leq\gamma/8. $$

Let $\Sigma_{0}$ denote the union of all closed components $\Lambda$ of $\Sigma$ contained an an open set $K_{\Lambda}\subset U$ diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{B}$ so that $\partial K_{\Lambda}\cap\Sigma=\varnothing$ .

Then $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{0})\leq 2E(\Omega)$ , and there are disjoint closed disks $D_{1},\ldots$ , $D_{p}$ satisfying

- (1) $D_{j}\subset\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{0}$ ,

- (2) $\partial D_{j}\subset\partial U^{\prime}$ ,

- (3)

$$ \left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}D_{j}\right)\cap U^{\prime}=(\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{0})\cap U^{\prime}, $$

- (4) there is an isotopy $\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ such that $\phi(t,x)=x$ for all $(t,x)\in[0,1]\times W$ , where $W$ is a neighborhood of $(\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{0})\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}(D_{j}\setminus\partial D_{j})$ , so that

$$ \bigcup_{j=1}^{p}(\phi(1,D_{j})\setminus\partial D_{j})\subset U^{\prime} $$

- (5)

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{p}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{j}))\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\Omega), $$

where $\Omega^{j}\subset U$ is the region bounded by $D_{j}\cup F_{\partial D_{j}}$ , which exists by the existence of the isotopy in (4).

#### Remark 13.4.

Let $K_{1},\ldots,K_{s}\subset U$ be open 3-balls with $\Sigma_{0}\subset\bigcup_{j=1}^{s}K_{j}$ and $\partial K_{j}\cap\Sigma=\varnothing$ .

For each $\varepsilon>0$ , there is an open set $\bigcup_{j=1}^{s}K_{j}\subset W\subset U$ and an isotopy $\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ satisfying

- • $W\cap(\Sigma\setminus\Sigma_{0})=\varnothing$ ,

- • $\phi(t,x)=x$ for all $(x,t)\in(M\setminus W)\times[0,1]$ ,

- • $\phi(t,W)\subset W$ ,

- • $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi(1,\Sigma_{0}))<\varepsilon$ ,

- • the union of the regions bounded by each component of $\phi(1,\Sigma_{0})$ (given by Lemma 4.2) has volume bounded by $\varepsilon$ ,

- • and each component of $\phi(1,\Sigma_{0})$ has diameter less than $\varepsilon$ .

Let $\tilde{\Omega}$ be the region given by deleting $\Sigma_{0}$ in $\Sigma$ . Each component that we collapse decreases $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ by Proposition 8.1, and we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{0})\leq 2E(\Omega) $$

and

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\tilde{\Omega})-\inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(1,\tilde{\Omega}))\leq E(\Omega). $$

Hence, the general case of Theorem 13.3 follows from the special case where $\Sigma_{0}=\varnothing$ , which we henceforth assume in the proof below.

#### Remark 13.5.

Since $\Omega^{j}\subset U$ and $\mathcal{H}^{3}(U)\leq\eta$ , we have by Proposition 8.1 that

$$ \mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{j})\leq c_{1}^{2/3}\eta^{1/3}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{\partial D_{j}})). $$

By our choice of $\eta$ , we have

$$ c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{j})\leq\frac{1}{2}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{\partial D_{j}})). $$

Then conclusion (5) of Theorem 13.3 implies

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{p}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j})\leq 3\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+2E(\Omega). $$

#### Proof of Theorem 13.3.

The proof follows exactly as in [MSY82, Theorem 2], with the additional step of keeping track of volumes.

We induct on $q$ , where the case $q=0$ is trivial.

Assume $\Omega$ satisfies

- • $\Sigma_{0}=\varnothing$ ,

- • $\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})\leq\gamma/8$ ,

- • $E(\Omega)\leq 3\gamma/8-\frac{3}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})$ ,

- • $\Sigma$ is strongly $\tilde{\gamma}$ irreducible for $\tilde{\gamma}=\gamma/4+4\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+\frac{4}{3}E(\Omega)$ .

Assume as an inductive hypothesis that the conclusions of the theorem are true for $\hat{\Omega}=\phi(1,\Omega)$ for some $\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ if it satisfies the above assumptions with $q-1$ in space of $q$ and $\hat{\Omega}$ in place of $\Omega$ .

Without loss of generality (by relabeling), we have $F_{q}\cap\Gamma_{j}=\varnothing$ for all $j\neq q$ . Since $\Sigma$ is strongly $\tilde{\gamma}$ -irreducible and $\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})<\tilde{\gamma}$ , there is a disk $D\subset\Sigma$ so that $\partial D=\Gamma_{q}$ and $\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)<\delta^{2}/2$ . Then $D\cup F_{q}$ is homeomorphic to $S^{2}$ and $\mathcal{H}^{2}(D\cup F_{q})<\delta^{2}/2+\delta^{2}/2=\delta^{2}$ , so Lemma 4.2 implies that $D\cup F_{q}=\partial K$ for $K\subset U$ an open 3-ball. Let $\Lambda$ be the component of $\Sigma$ containing $D$ . Since $\Sigma_{0}=\varnothing$ by assumption, we have $\Lambda\setminus D\not\subset K$ . Hence, we have $(\Sigma\setminus D)\cap K=\varnothing$ (because $\Sigma\setminus D$ does not intersect $F_{q}$ ).

Let $\Sigma_{*}=(\Sigma\setminus D)\cup F_{q}$ and $\Omega_{*}$ the corresponding region. As in [MSY82, Theorem 2], for every $\varepsilon>0$ , there is a continuous isotopy $\alpha$ taking $\Sigma_{*}$ to a smooth surface $\hat{\Sigma}_{*}$ and $\Omega_{*}$ to $\hat{\Omega}_{*}$ satisfying

- • $\hat{\Omega}_{*}=\phi(1,\Omega)$ for some $\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ ,

- • $\hat{\Sigma}_{*}\cap\partial U^{\prime}=\bigcup_{j=1}^{q-1}\Gamma_{j}$ ,

- • $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\hat{\Sigma}_{*}\triangle\Sigma)<\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})+\varepsilon$ ,

- • $\mathcal{H}^{3}(\hat{\Omega}_{*}\triangle\Omega)<\mathcal{H}^{3}(K)+\varepsilon/(2c)$ ,

- • $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\hat{\Sigma}_{*})<\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})-\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\varepsilon/2$ ,

- • $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\hat{\Sigma}_{*})\geq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{*})$ .

Using $\mathcal{H}^{3}(U)\leq\eta/8$ , Proposition 8.1 implies $c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K)\leq\frac{1}{4}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(D))$ . We assume $\varepsilon\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})/4$ . Observe that since $\Omega$ and $\hat{\Omega}_{*}$ are in the same isotopy class, we have

$$ \displaystyle E(\hat{\Omega}_{*}) \displaystyle<E(\Omega)+c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})-\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)+\varepsilon \displaystyle\leq E(\Omega)+\frac{3}{2}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})-\frac{3}{4}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D). $$

By [MSY82, Remark 3.11], we have that $\hat{\Sigma}_{*}$ is strongly $\gamma^{*}$ -irreducible, where

$$ \displaystyle\gamma^{*} \displaystyle=\gamma/4+4\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+\frac{4}{3}E(\Omega)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)-2\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q}) \displaystyle=\gamma/4+4\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+\frac{4}{3}E(\Omega)+2\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})-\mathcal{H}^{2}(D) \displaystyle\geq\gamma/4+4\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+\frac{4}{3}E(\hat{\Omega}_{*}). $$

Furthermore, we have

$$ \displaystyle E(\hat{\Omega}_{*}) \displaystyle\leq E(\Omega)+\frac{3}{2}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q}) \displaystyle\leq 3\gamma/8-\frac{3}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+\frac{3}{2}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q}) \displaystyle=3\gamma/8-\frac{3}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j}). $$

Hence, $\hat{\Omega}_{*}$ satisfies the inductive hypothesis. Then there are pairwise disjoint disks $\tilde{\Delta}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{\Delta}_{p}$ satisfying

- • $\tilde{\Delta}_{j}\subset\hat{\Sigma}_{*}$ ,

- • $\partial\tilde{\Delta}_{j}\subset\partial U^{\prime}$ ,

- •

$$ \left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}\tilde{\Delta}_{j}\right)\cap U^{\prime}=\hat{\Sigma}_{*}\cap U^{\prime}, $$

- • there is an isotopy $\tilde{\psi}\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ such that $\tilde{\psi}(t,x)=x$ for all $(t,x)\in[0,1]\times\tilde{W}$ , where $\tilde{W}$ is a neighborhood of $\hat{\Sigma}_{*}\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}(\tilde{\Delta}_{j}\setminus\partial\tilde{\Delta}_{j})$ , so that

$$ \bigcup_{j=1}^{p}(\tilde{\psi}(1,\tilde{\Delta}_{j})\setminus\partial\tilde{\Delta}_{j})\subset U^{\prime}, $$

- •

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{p}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Delta}_{j})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\tilde{\Omega}^{j}))\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\hat{\Omega}_{*}). $$

Letting $\Delta_{j}\coloneqq(\alpha^{-1})(1,\tilde{\Delta}_{j})$ (i.e. the time-reversal of the smoothing isotopy $\alpha$ for $\Sigma_{*}$ ), and taking $\psi\coloneqq\tilde{\psi}*\alpha$ (i.e. the concatenation of isotopies), we have that

- • $\Delta_{j}\subset\Sigma_{*}$ ,

- • $\partial\Delta_{j}\subset\partial U^{\prime}$ ,

- •

$$ \left(\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}\Delta_{j}\right)\cap U^{\prime}=\Sigma_{*}\cap U^{\prime}, $$

- • there is an isotopy $\psi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ such that $\psi(t,x)=x$ for all $(t,x)\in[0,1]\times W^{\prime}$ , where $W^{\prime}$ is a neighborhood of $\Sigma_{*}\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}(\Delta_{j}\setminus\partial\Delta_{j})$ , so that

$$ \bigcup_{j=1}^{p}(\psi(1,\Delta_{j})\setminus\partial\Delta_{j})\subset U^{\prime}, $$

- •

$$ \sum_{j=1}^{p}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Delta_{j})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\tilde{\Omega}^{j}))\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\hat{\Omega}_{*}). $$

Let $\beta$ be a continuous isotopy so that $\beta(t,K)\subset K$ , $\beta|_{\{t\}\times\Sigma\setminus D}=\mathbf{1}_{\Sigma\setminus D}$ , and $\beta(1,D)=F_{q}$ . Consider the following two cases:

Case 1: $F_{q}\subset\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}\Delta_{j}$ . Select the disks $D_{1},\ldots,D_{p}$ by taking $D_{j_{0}}=(\Delta_{j_{0}}\setminus F_{q})\cup D$ for the unique $j_{0}$ so that $F_{q}\subset\Delta_{j_{0}}$ , and $D_{j}=\Delta_{j}$ for $j\neq j_{0}$ . Define an isotopy by $\tilde{\phi}=\psi*\beta$ . By smoothing $\tilde{\phi}$ , we obtain the desired isotopy $\phi$ . We compute

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{j})) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{p}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Delta_{j})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\tilde{\Omega}^{j}))+\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K)+\varepsilon \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\hat{\Omega}_{*})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)-\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K)+\varepsilon \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\Omega)+2\varepsilon \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\Omega)+2\varepsilon. $$

Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, the desired inequality holds.

Case 2: $F_{q}\not\subset\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}\Delta_{j}$ . Define the disks $D_{1},\ldots,D_{p+1}$ by $D_{j}=\Delta_{j}$ for $j<p+1$ and $D_{p+1}=D$ . Define an isotopy $\tilde{\phi}=\hat{\beta}*\psi*\beta$ , where $\hat{\beta}\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ satisfies $\hat{\beta}(t,x)=x$ for all $(x,t)\in(\Sigma\setminus D)\times[0,1]$ and $\hat{\beta}(1,F_{q})$ is a disk $\tilde{D}\subset U^{\prime}$ with $\partial\tilde{D}=\partial D$ , $\tilde{D}\cap\partial U^{\prime}=\partial\tilde{D}$ , and $\tilde{D}\cap\psi(t,\Sigma_{*})=\Gamma_{q}$ for all $t\in[0,1]$ . We claim that in this case there is a neighborhood $W$ of $\partial D=\Gamma_{q}$ so that $W\cap D\subset U^{\prime}$ . Otherwise we would have $W$ with $W\supset\partial D$ and $W\cap(\Sigma\setminus D)\subset U^{\prime}$ , which would imply $F_{q}\subset\bigcup_{j=1}^{p}\Delta_{j}$ , a contradiction. By smoothing $\tilde{\phi}$ , we obtain the required isotopy. We compute

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p+1}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{j})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\Omega^{j})) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{p}(\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Delta_{j})-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(\tilde{\Omega}^{j}))+\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K)+\varepsilon \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\hat{\Omega}_{*})+\mathcal{H}^{2}(D)-c\mathcal{H}^{3}(K)+\varepsilon \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\Omega)+\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{q})+2\varepsilon \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mathcal{H}^{2}(F_{j})+E(\Omega)+2\varepsilon. $$

Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, the desired inequality holds. ∎

#### 13.3. Gamma-reduction of minimizing sequence

We now modify the initial minimizing sequence $\{\Sigma_{k}\}$ to a new sequence $\{\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}\}$ with $\lim\mathbf{v}(\tilde{\Sigma}_{k})=\lim\mathbf{v}(\Sigma_{k})=V$ so that each $\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}$ is strongly $(\gamma,U)$ -irreducible for some $\gamma$ .

For $q\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\gamma\in(0,\delta^{2}/9)$ , let $k_{q}(\gamma)$ be the largest integer such that there exist $\Sigma_{q}^{(j)}\in\mathcal{C}(\Sigma_{q},U)$ for $j=1,\ldots,k_{q}(\gamma)$ with

$$ \Sigma_{q}^{(k_{q}(\gamma))}\overset{(\gamma,U)}{<}\ldots\overset{(\gamma,U)}{<}\Sigma_{q}^{(2)}\overset{(\gamma,U)}{<}\Sigma_{q}^{(1)}=\Sigma_{q}. $$

We claim that $k_{q}(\gamma)$ is bounded independent of $q$ and $\gamma$ . Indeed, there is an upper bound on the topology of $\Sigma_{q}$ and $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{q})$ independent of $q$ and $W$ by assumption. Then the uniform bound on $k_{q}(\gamma)$ follows from [MSY82, (3.9)].

We also note that $k_{q}(\gamma)\leq k_{q}(\gamma^{\prime})$ for $\gamma<\gamma^{\prime}$ , which follows by definition.

Let $l(\gamma)$ be the nonnegative integer defined by

$$ l(\gamma)\coloneqq\limsup_{q\to\infty}k_{q}(\gamma). $$

$l$ is an nondecreasing integer-valued function of $\gamma$ , so there is $\gamma_{0}\in(0,\delta^{2}/9)$ so that

$$ l(\gamma)=l(\gamma_{0})\ \text{for\ all}\ \gamma\in(0,\gamma_{0}]. $$

For each $n\geq\gamma_{0}^{-1}$ , there is a $q_{n}\geq n$ so that $k_{q_{n}}(1/n)=l(1/n)=l(\gamma_{0})$ . We set

$$ \tilde{\Sigma}_{n}\coloneqq\Sigma_{q_{n}}^{(k_{q_{n}}(1/n))}. $$

Hence, $\tilde{\Sigma}_{n}$ is strongly $(\gamma_{0},U)$ -irreducible for all sufficiently large $n$ .

By [MSY82, (3.10)], we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\Sigma}_{n}\triangle\Sigma_{q_{n}})\leq C/n $$

for some $C$ independent of $n$ . Hence, $\lim\mathbf{v}(\tilde{\Sigma}_{n})=\lim\mathbf{v}(\Sigma_{k})$ .

Let $\tilde{\Omega}_{n}\subset M$ be the open set corresponding to $\tilde{\Sigma}_{n}$ (which is obtained from $\Omega_{q_{n}}$ in the obvious way at each $(\gamma,U)$ -reduction). Moreover, since $\Sigma_{q_{n}}$ can be recovered from $\tilde{\Sigma}_{n}$ be deleting disks and adding thin tubes, we have

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\tilde{\Omega}_{n})\leq\inf_{\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(1,\tilde{\Omega}_{n}))+\varepsilon_{n}^{\prime} $$

where $\varepsilon_{n}^{\prime}\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ .

### 14. Interior Regularity

We prove the interior regularity part of Theorem 1.1. To clarify, the “sufficiently small” assumption on $U$ is $\mathcal{H}^{3}(U)\leq\eta/8$ , where $\eta$ is defined in (8.1).

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1 Interior Regularity.

$$ \rho^{-1}\int_{\rho/2}^{\rho}\mathcal{H}^{1}(\Sigma_{k}\cap\partial B_{s}(x_{0}))\ ds\leq C\rho $$

for all sufficiently large $k$ , where $C$ depends on $\mu$ , $\rho_{0}(x_{0})$ , and $\|V\|(U)$ . Then there is a sequence $\rho_{k}\in(3\rho/4,\rho)$ so that $\Sigma_{k}$ has transverse intersection with $\partial B_{\rho_{k}}(x_{0})$ and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{1}(\Sigma_{k}\cap\partial B_{\rho_{k}}(x_{0}))\leq C\rho\leq C\eta_{1}\rho_{0}(x_{0}) $$

for all sufficiently large $k$ , provided $\rho\leq\eta_{1}\rho_{0}(x_{0})$ for some $\eta_{1}\in(0,1)$ to be determined. For $\eta_{1}$ sufficiently small and $k$ sufficiently large, we can apply Theorem 13.3 to $\Sigma_{k}$ with $U^{\prime}=B_{\rho_{k}}(x_{0})$ . Hence, there are disks $D_{k}^{(1)},\ldots,D_{k}^{(q_{k})}\subset\Sigma_{k}$ and isotopies $\phi^{(k)}\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ so that for $k$ sufficiently large, we have

- • $\partial D_{k}^{(l)}\subset\partial B_{\rho_{k}}(x_{0})$ ,

- • $\Sigma_{k}\cap B_{\rho_{k}}(x_{0})=(\bigcup_{l=1}^{q_{k}}D_{k}^{(l)})\cap B_{\rho_{k}}(x_{0})$ ,

- • $\phi^{(k)}(1,D_{k}^{(l)})\setminus\partial D_{k}^{(l)}\subset B_{\rho_{k}}(x_{0})$ ,

- • $\sum_{l=1}^{q_{k}}\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k}^{(l)})\leq\tilde{C}\eta_{1}^{2}\rho_{0}(x_{0})^{2}$ (see (13.1)).

For $\eta_{1}$ sufficiently small and $k$ sufficiently large, we can apply Lemma 8.2 to produce disks $\tilde{D}_{k}^{(l)}$ with $\partial\tilde{D}_{k}^{(l)}=\partial D_{k}^{(l)}$ , $\tilde{D}_{k}^{(l)}\setminus\partial D_{k}^{(l)}\subset B_{\rho_{k}}(x_{0})$ , and

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{D}_{k}^{(l)})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(D_{k}^{(l)})+T_{h}(\tilde{D}_{k}^{(l)},D_{k}^{(l)}). $$

By taking a subsequence, we can assume that $\rho_{k}\to\rho_{\infty}$ . Take an arbitrary $\alpha>0$ small. We can construct oriented smooth disks $\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}\in\mathcal{D}^{*}(B_{\rho_{\infty}-\alpha}(x_{0}))$ so that (for all $k$ sufficiently large)

- • $\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}\cap B_{\rho_{\infty}-\alpha}(x_{0})=\bigcup_{l}\tilde{D}_{k}^{(l)}\cap B_{\rho_{\infty}-\alpha}(x_{0})$ ,

- • $\partial\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}\cap\overline{B}_{\rho_{\infty}-\alpha}(x_{0})=\varnothing$ ,

- • $\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}\setminus B_{\rho_{\infty}-\alpha}(x_{0})$ is connected.

Indeed, we can inductively add bridges outside $B_{\rho_{\infty}-\alpha}(x_{0})$ joining the disks $\tilde{D}_{k}^{(l)}$ . Then $\tilde{\Sigma}_{k}$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 10.2 with the set $B_{\rho_{\infty}-\alpha}(x_{0})$ . Hence, the interior regularity of Theorem 1.1 follows. ∎

### 15. Boundary Regularity

We prove the boundary regularity part of Theorem 1.1. We follow the proof of [DLP10].

#### 15.1. Wedge property

#### Definition 15.1.

Let $U=B_{\rho}(x)\subset M$ for $\rho\ll 1$ and let $\sigma\subset\partial U$ be a disjoint union of finitely many smooth Jordan curves. An open set $A\subset U$ meets $\partial U$ in $\sigma$ transversally if there is a positive angle $\theta_{0}$ so that

- • $\partial A\cap\partial U\subset\sigma$ ,

- • for every $p\in\partial A\cap\partial U$ , if we choose coordinates so that $T_{p}\partial U=\{z=0\}$ and $T_{p}\sigma=\{y=z=0\}$ , then every point $q=(q_{1},q_{2},q_{3})\in A$ satisfies $\frac{q_{3}}{q_{2}}\geq\tan(1/2-\theta_{0})$ .

#### Lemma 15.2 (Wedge Property).

There is a $r_{0}<1$ so that the following holds for $\rho<r_{0}$ . Let $V$ and $\Sigma:=\partial\Omega_{0}\cap U$ as in Theorem 1.1. Then there exists an open set $A\subset U$ which meets $\partial U$ in $\partial\Sigma$ transversally and satisfies $\mathrm{spt}\|V\|\subset\overline{A}$ .

We use the following result, see [DLP10, Lemma 5.3].

#### Proposition 15.3.

If $\beta\subset\partial B_{1}(0)\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is a disjoint union of finitely many $C^{2}$ Jordan curves, then the convex hull of $\beta$ meets $\partial B_{1}(0)$ in $\beta$ transversally.

#### Proof of Lemma 15.2.

Consider the rescaled exponential coordinates induced by the chart $f_{x,\rho}:\overline{B}_{\rho}(x)\to\overline{B}_{1}(0)$ given by $f_{x,\rho}(z)=(\exp_{x}^{-1}(z))/\rho$ . We apply Proposition 15.3 and let $B$ be the convex hull of $\beta=f(\partial\Sigma)$ .

Fix $\xi\in\beta$ and let $\pi_{1}$ and $\pi_{2}$ be the halfplanes delimiting the wedge of $B$ . We assume without loss of generality that $\pi_{1}=\{x_{3}\leq a\}$ for some $a\in(0,1)$ .

Let $C_{t}=(0,0,-t)$ , and let $S_{t}=B_{2}(C_{t})$ . Assuming $\rho$ is sufficiently small, (6.4) implies $\|\delta(f_{\#}V)\|\leq\|f_{\#}V\|$ . By [Whi10, Theorem 7], $\text{spt}\|V\|$ is contained is $\overline{S}_{t_{0}}$ , where $t_{0}$ is such that $\partial S_{t_{0}}\cap\partial B_{1}(0)\subset\pi_{1}$ . The same argument applies to $\pi_{2}$ and $\xi$ is arbitrary, so the conclusion follows. ∎

#### 15.2. Tangent cones at the boundary

Let $x\in\partial U$ . As in the previous section, consider the chart $f_{x,\rho}:B_{\rho}(x)\to B_{1}(0)$ given by $f_{x,\rho}(z)=(\exp_{x}^{-1}(z))/\rho$ . Fix coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ so that $f_{x,\rho}(U\cap B_{\rho}(x))$ converges to the half ball $B_{1}^{+}(0)=B_{1}(0)\cap\{x_{1}>0\}$ as $\rho\to 0$ .

We first follow the ideas of [DLR18, Lemma 6.4].

#### Lemma 15.4.

$\|V\|(\partial\Sigma)=0$ .

#### Proof.

Let $V^{r}=V\llcorner G_{2}(\overline{U}\setminus\partial\Sigma)$ and $V^{s}=V-V^{r}$ .

Let $X$ be a compactly supported vector field on $\overline{U}$ that vanishes on $\partial\Sigma$ . Let $\phi_{\delta}\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\overline{U}\setminus\partial\Sigma)$ satisfy

- • $\phi_{\delta}=1$ outside $B_{2\delta}(\partial\Sigma)$ ,

- • $|\nabla\phi_{\delta}|\leq C\delta^{-1}$ .

Since $X$ vanishes on $\partial\Sigma$ , we have $|X|\leq C\delta$ in $B_{2\delta}(\partial\Sigma)$ . Hence, $|\nabla(\phi_{\delta}X)|\leq C$ . Then by dominated convergence and the fact that $V$ has bounded first variation in $\overline{U}\setminus\partial\Sigma$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\delta V^{r}(X) \displaystyle=\int_{\overline{U}}\mathrm{div}_{\pi}X(p)\ dV^{r}(p,\pi) \displaystyle=\lim_{\delta\to 0}\int_{\overline{U}}\mathrm{div}_{\pi}(\phi_{\delta}X)(p)\ dV^{r}(p,\pi) \displaystyle=\lim_{\delta\to 0}\int_{\overline{U}}\mathrm{div}_{\pi}(\phi_{\delta}X)(p)\ dV(p,\pi) \displaystyle=\lim_{\delta\to 0}\int_{\overline{U}}H_{V}\cdot(\phi_{\delta}X)(p)\ dV(p,\pi) \displaystyle=\lim_{\delta\to 0}\int_{\overline{U}}H_{V}\cdot X(p)\ dV(p,\pi)=\delta V(X). $$

Hence, $\delta V^{s}=0$ .

Let $W$ be a small tubular neighborhood of $\partial\Sigma$ . For each $p\in W\setminus\partial\Sigma$ , let $q$ be the unique nearest point in $\partial\Sigma$ . Let $X(p)$ be the tangent vector at $p$ to the minimizing geodesic joining $p$ to $q$ parametrized on $[0,1]$ . Set $X(p)=0$ for $p\in\partial\Sigma$ . If $e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}$ is a smooth orthonormal frame over $\partial\Sigma$ with $e_{1}$ tangent to $\partial\Sigma$ , we have $\nabla_{e_{1}}X=0$ , $\nabla_{e_{2}}X=-e_{2}$ , and $\nabla_{e_{3}}X=-e_{3}$ along $\partial\Sigma$ . For any 2-plane $\pi$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{div}_{\pi}X(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{2}g(\nabla_{f_{i}}X,f_{i}) $$

for $\{f_{i}\}$ an orthonormal basis for $\pi$ . Hence, $\mathrm{div}_{\pi}X(p)\leq-1$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle 0=\delta V^{s}(X) \displaystyle=\int_{\overline{U}}\mathrm{div}_{\pi}X(p)\ dV^{s}(p,\pi)\leq-\|V^{s}\|(\overline{U})=-\|V\|(\partial\Sigma), $$

so $\|V\|(\partial\Sigma)=0$ . ∎

By Lemma 15.4, we can apply Allard’s boundary monotonicity formula [All75, 3.4(2)]. Then the varifolds $V_{x,\rho}\coloneqq(f_{x,\rho})_{\#}V$ have uniformly bounded mass with respect to $\rho$ . Hence, if we take a sequence $\rho_{j}\to\infty$ , there is a subsequence (not relabeled) so that $V_{x,\rho_{j}}\to W$ . We note by [Sim83, Theorem 42.7] that $W$ is stationary in $B_{1}^{+}(0)$ .

By Lemma 15.2, there is a positive angle $\theta_{0}$ so that (after changing coordinates) $\|W\|$ is supported in $\{|x_{2}|\leq x_{1}\tan(\theta_{0})\}$ . Then $\text{spt}\|W\|\cap\{x_{1}=0\}=\{x_{1}=x_{2}=0\}=:l$ .

By the same argument as Lemma 15.4, we have $\|W\|(l)=0$ . Hence, by Allard’s boundary monotonicity formula [All75, 3.4(2)], we have

$$ \|W\|(B_{\rho}(0))=\pi\theta(\|V\|,x)\rho^{2} $$

By Allard’s reflection principle [All75, 3.2], we have $W^{\prime}\coloneqq W+r_{\#}W$ is stationary. By (15.1) and [All72, §5.1, Corollary 2], $W^{\prime}$ is a cone, which implies $W$ is a cone.

By Allard’s boundary regularity theorem (see [All75, §4]), it suffices to show that any such $W$ is a half-disk of the form

$$ P_{\theta}\coloneqq\{y_{2}=y_{1}\tan(\theta)\}\cap B_{1}^{+}(0) $$

for some $\theta\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ .

By the classification of one dimensional stationary integral varifolds from [AA76], we have

$$ W=\sum_{i=1}^{N}k_{i}P_{\theta_{i}} $$

for $\theta_{i}\in[-\theta_{0},\theta_{0}]$ and $k_{i}\in\mathbb{N}$ . It therefore remains to show $N=1$ and $k_{1}=1$ .

#### 15.3. Reduction to the area minimization case

Consider a subsequence so that

$$ S_{n}\coloneqq f_{x_{0},\rho_{n}}(\Sigma_{k_{n}}\cap B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0})) $$

converges to $W$ . We further suppose that $\rho_{n}^{-2}\varepsilon_{k_{n}}\to 0$ . For any isotopy $\phi$ supported in $B_{1}^{+}(0)$ , let $\tilde{\phi}$ be the isotopy of $B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0})\cap U$ given by conjugating with the chart $f_{x_{0},\rho_{n}}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k_{n}}\cap B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0}))-\int_{\Omega_{k_{n}}\cap B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0})\cap U}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3} \displaystyle\hskip 56.9055pt\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\phi}(1,\Sigma_{k_{n}}\cap B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0})))-\int_{\tilde{\phi}(1,\Omega_{k_{n}}\cap B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0})\cap U)}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}+\varepsilon_{k_{n}}. $$

Since

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{k_{n}}\cap B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0}))=\rho_{n}^{2}\mathcal{H}^{2}(S_{n})+o(\rho_{n}^{2}), \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{2}(\tilde{\phi}(1,\Sigma_{k_{n}}\cap B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0})))=\rho_{n}^{2}\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi(1,S_{n}))+o(\rho_{n}^{2}), \displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{3}(B_{\rho_{n}}(x_{0})\cap U)=\rho_{n}^{3}\mathcal{H}^{3}(B_{1}^{+}(0))+o(\rho_{n}^{3})=o(\rho_{n}^{2}), $$

we have

$$ \mathcal{H}^{2}(S_{n})\leq\mathcal{H}^{2}(\phi(1,S_{n}))+\varepsilon_{n}^{\prime}, $$

where $\varepsilon_{n}^{\prime}\to 0$ . Hence, $S_{n}$ is $\varepsilon_{n}^{\prime}$ -area minimizing in its isotopy class, so the rest of the proof follows exactly as in [DLP10, §8]. Therefore, the boundary regularity of Theorem 1.1 follows.

## Part III Estimates and compactness for minimizers

We develop a compactness theory to prove an analogue of the curvature estimates for stable surfaces that works in our lower regularity setting.

### 16. $C^{1,1}$ Compactness

Let $U\subset M$ be a precompact open set with $C^{1}$ boundary. Recall from §4.1 that the map $\phi_{x}:\overline{B}_{\rho_{0}}^{T_{x}M}(0)\to\overline{B}_{\rho_{0}}^{M}(x)$ is the diffeomorphism defined by the exponential map for $x\in M$ .

Let $\Sigma^{2}$ be a compact orientable surface (possibly with boundary) and let $f:\Sigma\to M^{3}$ be 2-sided $C^{1,1}$ immersion such that $f(\Sigma)\subset U$ and $f(\partial\Sigma)\subset\partial U$ . Let $\nu:\Sigma\to TM$ denote a (Lipschitz) choice of unit normal vector field for the immersion. We endow $\Sigma$ with the pullback metric $f^{*}g$ and for $p\in\Sigma$ , we denote by $\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma}_{r}(p)$ the image $f(B^{\Sigma}_{r}(p))\subset M$ of the ball of radius $r$ centered at $p$ in $\Sigma$ .

Note that, since $f$ is a $C^{1,1}$ immersion, for any $p\in\Sigma$ there is $0<\rho(p)\leq\rho_{0}$ such that if $\Sigma_{p}$ is the component of $f^{-1}(B^{M}_{\rho(p)}(f(p)))$ which contains $p$ , then

- • $\Sigma_{p}\cap\partial\Sigma=\varnothing$ ,

- • $f$ is injective on $\Sigma_{p}$ ,

- • and $\phi^{-1}_{f(p)}(f(\Sigma_{p}))$ can be represented as the graph of a $C^{1,1}$ function $u_{p}$ over an open set $B_{p}\subset df_{p}(T_{f(p)}\Sigma)\subset T_{f(p)}M$ containing 0.

Then, for any $p\in\Sigma$ we can define the pointwise Lipschitz constant $\Lip_{p}\nu$ of $\nu$ to be the following quantity

$$ \Lip_{p}\nu\coloneqq\limsup_{B_{p}\ni\xi\to 0}\frac{|\nu_{p}(0)-\nu_{p}(\xi)|}{|\xi|} $$

where

- • $\nu_{p}:B_{p}\to T_{f(p)}M$ is the unit normal to the graph of $u_{p}$ in $(T_{f(p)}M,\phi_{f(p)}^{*}g)$ ,

- • gradients and distances are taken with respect to the pullback metric on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ .

#### Remark 16.1.

It is easy to see that for every $p\in\Sigma$ there is $0<r(p)\leq\rho(p)$ such that for any $\xi,\eta\in\phi_{x}^{-1}(\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma}_{r(p)}(p))$ we have

$$ |\nu_{p}(\xi)-\nu_{p}(\eta)|\leq 2\Lip_{p}\nu\,|\xi-\eta|. $$

To simplify the notation, we redefine $\rho(p)$ to be the same as $r(p)$ .

We start by proving a simple technical fact, which plays the same role in the proof of compactness as [CM11, Lemma 2.4].

#### Lemma 16.2.

Let $\Sigma^{2}$ be a compact orientable surface (possibly with boundary) and let $f:\Sigma\to M^{3}$ be 2-sided $C^{1,1}$ immersion such that $f(\Sigma)\subset U$ and $f(\partial\Sigma)\subset\partial U$ . Let $\nu:\Sigma\to TM$ be a (Lipschitz) choice of unit normal vector field for the immersion such that $\sup_{p\in\Sigma}\Lip_{p}\nu\leq C_{0}$ . Then, for any $K\subset\subset U$ there is $r_{K}=r_{K}(\rho_{0},\dist_{M}(K,\partial U),C_{0})>0$ such that if $x=f(p)\in f(\Sigma)\cap K$ and $r\leq r_{K}$ , then

- (1) $\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma}_{2r}(p)$ can be written as the graph of a $C^{1,1}$ function $u$ over an open neighborhood of $0$ in $df_{p}(T_{p}\Sigma)\subset T_{x}M$ , such that $|\nabla u|\leq 1$ and $\Lip\nabla u\leq 2\sqrt{2}C_{0}$ ,

- (2) the connected component of $f^{-1}(B^{M}_{r}(x))$ containing $p$ is contained in $B^{\Sigma}_{2r}(p)$ .

#### Proof.

Since $K\subset\subset U$ , then $\delta_{K}\coloneqq\mathrm{dist}_{M}(K,\partial U)>0$ . Hence $\dist_{f(\Sigma)}(f(\Sigma)\cap K,f(\partial\Sigma))\geq\delta_{K}>0$ . Let $r\leq\min\{\rho_{0}/2,\delta_{K}/2\}>0$ and let $p\in\Sigma$ be such that $x=f(p)\in f(\Sigma)\cap K$ . Then $\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma}_{r}(p)\subset B^{M}_{r}(x)\subset\subset U$ stays a fixed positive distance away from $\partial U$ .

Now, let $y=f(q)\in\mathcal{B}_{r}^{\Sigma}(p)$ and let $\tilde{\gamma}:[0,1]\to\Sigma$ be a curve from $p$ to $q$ in $\Sigma$ such that $\gamma=f\circ\tilde{\gamma}$ is a minimizing constant speed geodesic from $x$ to $y$ in $f(\Sigma)$ .

By compactness, we can pick $0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots<t_{N}<t_{N+1}=1$ so that the segment $\overline{x_{j}x_{j+1}}=\gamma([t_{j},t_{j+1}])\subset\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma}_{r}(p)$ (which is a minimizing geodesic from $x_{j}=f(p_{j})$ to $x_{j+1}=f(p_{j+1})$ ) lies in $f(\Sigma_{p_{j}})$ for $j=0,\dots,N$ . Hence, by (4.1) and Remark 16.1,

$$ \displaystyle|d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(p_{j})-d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(p_{j+1})| \displaystyle\leq 4|d\phi_{x_{j}}^{-1}\nu(p_{j})-d\phi_{x_{j}}^{-1}\nu(p_{j+1})| \displaystyle\leq 8\,(\Lip_{p_{j}}\nu)\,d_{\Sigma}(x,y)|t_{j}-t_{j+1}|, $$

and, using the uniform pointwise Lipschitz bound,

$$ \displaystyle|d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(p)-d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(q)| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=0}^{N}|d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(p_{j})-d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(p_{j+1})| \displaystyle\leq 8C_{0}\,d_{f(\Sigma)}(x,y)\sum_{j=0}^{N}|t_{j}-t_{j+1}| \displaystyle=8C_{0}\,d_{f(\Sigma)}(x,y) \displaystyle\leq 8C_{0}r. $$

In particular, this proves that for any $y=f(q)\in\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma}_{r}(p)$ , we have $|d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(p)-d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(q)|\leq 8C_{0}r$ . By taking $r\leq 2r_{K}\coloneqq\min\{\rho_{0}/2,\delta_{K}/2,\frac{1}{16C_{0}}\}$ , we have that

$$ |d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(p)-d\phi_{x}^{-1}\nu(q)|\leq\frac{1}{2} $$

for all $y=f(q)\in\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma}_{r}(p)$ , which implies that the whole of $\mathcal{B}^{\Sigma}_{r}(p)$ can be written as the graph of a $C^{1,1}$ function $u$ over an open subset of $df_{p}(T_{p}\Sigma)\subset T_{x}M$ .

Then it is immediate to see (as in [CM11, Lemma 2.4]) that $u$ satisfies $|\nabla u|\leq 1$ and $\Lip\nabla u\leq 2\sqrt{2}C_{0}$ .

The second statement follows from the first as in [CM11, Lemma 2.4]. ∎

The next lemma is essentially a geometric Arzelà-Ascoli theorem, and it follows indeed from the usual Arzelà-Ascoli compactness theorem. The argument is well-known and varitions of it appear in several difference sources and contexts (see for example [ACGL22, Theorem 11.8]). We shall now outline it for the sake of completeness.

#### Lemma 16.3.

Let $\{\Sigma_{i}\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of compact orientable surfaces and let $f_{i}:\Sigma_{i}\to U$ be a sequence of 2-sided $C^{1,1}$ immersions with unit normal vector field $\nu_{i}$ in a precompact open set $U\subset M$ with $f(\partial\Sigma_{i})\subset\partial U$ . If the immersions have locally bounded area, i.e. for every $K\subset\subset U$ there is a finite $c_{K}$ such that $\sup_{i}\mathcal{H}^{2}(f_{i}(\Sigma_{i})\cap K)\leq c_{K}$ , and

$$ C_{0}:=\sup_{i}\sup_{p\in\Sigma_{i}}\Lip_{p}\nu_{i}<\infty, $$

then there is a subsequence (not relabeled) so that $f_{i}$ converges in $C^{1,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}$ to a $C^{1,1}$ immersion $f:\Sigma\to U$ with $\sup_{p\in\Sigma}\mathrm{Lip}_{p}\nu\leq C_{0}$ .

#### Sketch of proof.

Let $K\subset\subset U$ . We can cover the compact set $\overline{K}$ with finitely many balls $\{B_{k}=B^{M}_{r_{K}/2}(z_{k})\}_{k=1}^{N}$ . Suppose $p_{i}\in\Sigma_{i}$ satisfies $f_{i}(p_{i})=x_{i}\in B_{k}$ . By Lemma 16.2, the component of $f_{i}^{-1}(B^{M}_{r_{K}/2}(x_{i}))$ is contained in $B_{r_{K}}^{\Sigma_{i}}(p_{i})$ and its image under $f_{i}$ is the graph of a $C^{1,1}$ function satisfying explicit $C^{1,1}$ -bounds depending only on $C_{0}$ (not on $i$ ). This image is the graph of a function $u_{i}$ such that $|\nabla u_{i}|\leq 1$ —in particular, it has area bounded from below by some uniform constant $\kappa r_{K}^{2}$ . By the uniform upper bounds on the area of $f_{i}(\Sigma_{i})$ in compact sets, we conclude that $f_{i}^{-1}(B_{k})$ is contained in at most $N_{0}$ balls of radius $r_{K}$ in $\Sigma_{i}$ , where $N_{0}$ is a constant depending only on $K$ , the area bounds, and $C_{0}$ (not on $i$ or $k$ ).

For any $k\in\{1,\dots,N\}$ , we can select a set of at most $N_{0}$ points $\{p_{l}^{i,k}\}_{l}\subset\Sigma_{i}$ so that $f_{i}^{-1}(B_{k})$ is covered by $\{B^{\Sigma_{i}}_{r_{K}}(p_{l}^{i,k})\}_{l}$ . Up to a subsequence we may assume as $i\to\infty$ that $f(p_{l}^{i,k})\to x_{l}^{k}$ and $df_{p_{l}^{i,k}}(T_{p_{l}^{i,k}}\Sigma_{i})\to P_{l}^{k}$ , a 2-dimensional subspace of $T_{x_{l}}M$ . Note that the corresponding graphical functions satisfy uniform $C^{1,1}$ bounds, so by Arzelà-Ascoli, up to a subsequence, they converge (in $C^{1,\alpha}$ for any $0<\alpha<1$ ) to some $C^{1,1}$ function $u_{l}^{k}$ defined on $B^{T_{x_{l}^{k}}M}_{r_{K}}(0)\cap P_{l}^{k}$ with the same $C^{1,1}$ bound.

We then repeat this argument for all $k=1,\dots,N$ and take a diagonal subsequence. It is clear that the graphs we obtained match up on the overlaps between balls (because the surfaces $f_{i}(\Sigma_{i})$ do), so we have produced our immersed limit surface restricted to $K\subset\subset U$ .

Lastly, we take an exhaustion of $U$ by compact sets, repeat this procedure inductively and check that the limit surfaces coincide on the overlaps. ∎

### 17. Curvature Estimates

We now use these compactness ideas to prove the curvature estimates.

For convenience, we denote by $\mathcal{P}$ the set of pairs $(V,\Omega)$ where $V$ is a varifold and $\Omega\subset M$ is a set of finite perimeter with the property that there is a sequence $\Omega_{j}\subset M$ with smooth boundary satisfying

$$ \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{j}}\xrightarrow{L^{1}}\mathbf{1}_{\Omega},\ \ D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{j}}\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega},\ \ \mathbf{v}(\partial\Omega_{j})\rightharpoonup V. $$

We let $\mathcal{P}_{c}$ denote the pairs $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}$ so that $V$ has $c$ -bounded first variation.

For $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}$ , we define

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(V,\Omega):=\|V\|(M)-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}. $$

#### Definition 17.1.

A pair $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}$ is a weakly stable $h$ -surface in $U$ if

- • $(V,\Omega)$ has the regularity of Theorem 1.1 in $U$ ,

- • for any $\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ , we have $\displaystyle\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(t,\cdot)_{\#}V,\phi(t,\Omega))=0,$ $\displaystyle\left.\frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}\right|_{t=0}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(t,\cdot)_{\#}V,\phi(t,\Omega))\geq 0.$

We check that weakly stable $h$ -surfaces satisfy the usual stability inequality.

#### Proposition 17.2.

If $(V,\Omega)$ is a weakly stable $h$ -surface in $U$ with corresponding immersion $f:\Sigma\to U$ , then for any $\psi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\Sigma)$ which is the pullback by $f$ of a smooth function on $U$ , we have

$$ \int_{\Sigma}|\nabla^{\Sigma}\psi|^{2}-(|A^{\Sigma}|^{2}+\mathrm{Ric}_{M}(\nu,\nu))\psi^{2}\ d\mathcal{H}^{2}\geq\int_{\partial^{*}\Omega}(H^{\Sigma}h+\partial_{\nu}h-|H^{\Sigma}|^{2})\psi^{2}\ d\mathcal{H}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

This formula follows from the standard computation of the second variation of area and potential energy (see [BdCE88, Proposition 2.5]), combined with the observation that all the integrands are well defined measurable and integrable functions since the immersion is $C^{1,1}$ . ∎

The next result is the $C^{1,1}$ analogue of the usual curvature estimates for stable minimal (or prescribed mean curvature) surfaces (see e.g. [ZZ20, Theorem 3.6]).

#### Theorem 17.3.

Let $U\subset M$ be an open set and $c>0$ . Let $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}_{c}$ be a weakly stable $h$ -surface in $U$ for a function with $\|h\|_{C^{1}}\leq c$ and $\|V\|(U)\leq m_{0}$ . Let $f:\Sigma\to U$ be the $C^{1,1}$ immersion inducing the varifold $V$ in $U$ . Then there is a constant $C=C(U,c,m_{0})>0$ so that

$$ \sup_{p\in\Sigma}\ \min\{1,d_{\Sigma}(p,f^{-1}(\partial U))\}\ \Lip_{p}\nu\leq C. $$

#### Proof.

We argue by contradiction, using a standard point-picking argument (cf. [Whi16, Lecture 3]).

Suppose there is a sequence of such immersions $f_{i}:\Sigma_{i}\to M$ so that

$$ \sup_{p\in\Sigma_{i}}\ \min\{1,d_{\Sigma_{i}}(p,f_{i}^{-1}(\partial U))\}\ \Lip_{p}\nu_{i}=R_{i}\to\infty. $$

Let us denote the local Lipschitz constant $\Lip_{p}\nu_{i}$ by $l_{i}(p)$ .

Now pick $p_{i}\in\Sigma_{i}$ so that

$$ \min\{1,d_{\Sigma_{i}}(p_{i},f_{i}^{-1}(\partial U))\}\ l_{i}(p_{i})\geq\frac{1}{2}R_{i}. $$

We shall rescale the metric on $U$ by $l_{i}(p_{i})\to\infty$ and obtain a new metric $\tilde{g}_{i}=l_{i}(p_{i})g$ , so that, with respect to the new metric, $\tilde{l}_{i}(p_{i})=1$ . By (17.2), the rescalings $(U,\tilde{g}_{i})$ converge locally smoothly to $(\mathbb{R}^{3},g_{\mathrm{Euc}})$ , and, under the rescaling,

$$ d_{\tilde{\Sigma}_{i}}(p_{i},f_{i}^{-1}(\partial U))\geq\frac{1}{2}R_{i}. $$

Assume, without loss of generality that $f_{i}(p_{i})\to 0\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . For $p,p_{i}\in\Sigma_{i}$ , if (under the rescaling) $d_{\tilde{\Sigma}_{i}}(p,p_{i})\leq\frac{1}{4}R_{i}$ , then, since the quantity $d_{\Sigma_{i}}(\cdot,f_{i}^{-1}(\partial U))\ l_{i}(\cdot)$ is scale invariant, $\tilde{l}_{i}(p)\leq\frac{R_{i}}{R_{i}/2-R_{i}/4}=4$ . Thus,

$$ \sup_{p\in B^{\tilde{\Sigma}_{i}}_{R_{i}/4}(p_{i})}\tilde{l}_{i}(p)\leq 4. $$

In any compact set, the mass bound $m_{0}$ and the mononicity formula give a uniform mass bound for the rescaled immersions. Recalling that $R_{i}\to\infty$ , we conclude that, by Lemma 16.3, (up to a subsequence) the rescaled immersions converge in $C^{1,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}$ to a complete, 2-sided $C^{1,1}$ immersion $f:\Sigma\to\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with Lipschitz unit normal vector field $\nu$ such that $\sup_{\Sigma}\,\Lip_{p}\nu\leq 4$ .

Claim 1: $f$ is a $C^{1,1}$ immersion with locally ordered sheets. Indeed, the $C^{1,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}$ graphical convergence preserves the local ordering of sheets of the immersions $f_{i}$ .

Claim 2: The image of $f$ is a smooth embedded minimal surface. Since each sheet of the rescaled immersion in a small ball has $c/R_{i}$ bounded first variation, the lower semicontinuity of the first variation (see [Sim83, Theorem 42.7]) implies that each sheet of $f$ in a small ball is stationary. By Allard’s regularity theorem [All72], $f$ is a smooth minimal immersion. Since the sheets are ordered locally, the strong maximum principle for minimal surfaces implies that each component of the image of $f$ is a smoothly embedded minimal surface.

Claim 3: $f$ is a stable minimal immersion. By claim 2, $f$ is a covering of a smooth minimal embedding, so we can assume without loss of generality that $f$ is an embedding. We consider the limit of (17.1), where we fix a function $\psi$ on $\Sigma$ with compact support and transplant it to $\Sigma_{i}$ using the graphical identification. Since the rescalings satisfy $|H^{\Sigma_{i}}|\leq c/R_{i}$ and $|\nabla h_{i}|\leq c/R_{i}$ , the right hand side of (17.1) vanishes in the limit. Since the convergence is $C^{1,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}$ , every term on the right hand side converges to the corresponding term for $\Sigma$ except the $|A^{\Sigma_{i}}|^{2}$ term. Since the ambient space converges locally smoothly to Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , [Lan85, Theorem 4.3] implies that the term $\int_{\Sigma_{i}}|A^{\Sigma_{i}}|^{2}u^{2}\ d\mathcal{H}^{2}$ is lower semicontinuous (we have local weak convergence in $W^{2,2}$ by the uniform $C^{1,1}$ bounds). Hence, $\Sigma$ satisfies the stability inequality in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ .

By the stable Bernstein theorem in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ due to [FCS80], [dCP79], and [Pog81], $\Sigma$ is flat. By Corollary 11.2, $\Sigma_{i}$ converges in $C^{1,1}_{\text{loc}}$ to the flat limit. However, we chose points so that $\text{Lip}_{p_{i}}\nu_{i}\geq 1$ where $p_{i}\to 0$ , which yields a contradiction. ∎

As usual, this estimate directly implies $C^{1,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}$ pre-compactness for weakly stable $h$ -surfaces (cf. [ZZ20, Theorem 3.6]).

## Part IV Application to existence in the 3-sphere

### 18. Min-Max Setup

We set up an appropriate setting to carry out the min-max procedure of [CDL03] for the prescribed mean curvature functional.

Let $v>0$ , $\kappa>0$ , and $c>0$ satisfy

$$ \frac{8\pi}{(1+\kappa)^{2}+c^{2}/4}>4\pi+vc. $$

Consider a smooth metric $g$ on $S^{3}$ so that

- • $R_{g}\geq 6$ ,

- • $\Ric(g)>0$ ,

- • $\mathrm{Vol}(S^{3},g)\leq v$ ,

- • $(S^{3},g)$ isometrically embeds in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ with $|A_{S^{3}}|\leq 1+\kappa$ .

Note that the round metric satisfies these conditions with $v=2\pi^{2}$ , $\kappa=0$ , and $c=0.547$ . Moreover, there is an explicit $C^{2}$ graphical neighborhood of the standard embedding $\mathbf{S}^{3}\subset\mathbb{R}^{4}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}$ and an explicit constant $c>0$ for which these conditions are satisfied (by rescaling). Let $h:S^{3}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function with $|h|\leq c$ . Moreover, we assume that $h$ satisfies the conditions (†) or (‡) from [ZZ20]. By [ZZ20, Proposition 3.8 and Corollary 3.18], the set of functions satisfying these conditions is open and dense, all positive functions satisfy (‡), and any such function $h$ has the unique continuation property for surfaces of prescribed mean curvature $h$ .

Let $g_{0}$ be the round metric on $S^{3}$ . Let $x_{0}\in S^{3}$ . Let $\{\Omega_{t}\}_{t\in[0,1]}$ be given by

$$ \Omega_{t}:=B_{\pi t}^{g_{0}}(x_{0}). $$

Note that we use the round metric in particular only to define the standard sweepout; everything else uses the general metric $g$ . Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the set of smooth maps $\psi:[0,1]\times[0,1]\times S^{3}\to S^{3}$ so that

- • $\psi(s,t,\cdot)$ is a diffeomorphism of $S^{3}$ ,

- • $\psi(0,t,\cdot)=\mathrm{id}$ .

We define the min-max width $\omega_{1}(g,h)$ by

$$ \omega_{1}(g,h):=\inf_{\psi\in\mathcal{M}}\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\psi(1,t,\Omega_{t})). $$

We say $\{\Omega_{t}^{j}=\psi_{j}(1,t,\Omega_{t})\}_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ for $\psi_{j}\in\mathcal{M}$ is a minimizing sequence if

$$ \lim_{j\to\infty}\sup_{t}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega_{t}^{j})=\omega_{1}(g,h). $$

Given a minimizing sequence, we say $\{\Omega_{t_{j}}^{j}\}$ is a min-max sequence if

$$ \lim_{j\to\infty}\mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega_{t_{j}}^{j})=\omega_{1}(g,h). $$

By the standard compactness theory (see [Mag12, Theorem 12.26] and [Sim83, Chapter 1, Theorem 4.4]), for any min-max sequence $\{\Omega_{t_{j}}^{j}\}$ , there is a set $\Omega\subset S^{3}$ and a varifold $V$ satisfying

$$ \mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{t_{j}}^{j}}\xrightarrow{L^{1}}\mathbf{1}_{\Omega},\ \ D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega_{t_{j}}^{j}}\overset{\ast}{\rightharpoonup}D\mathbf{1}_{\Omega},\ \ \mathbf{v}(\partial\Omega_{t_{j}}^{j})\rightharpoonup V, $$

and

$$ \|V\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}=\omega_{1}(g,h). $$

We show the following theorem.

#### Theorem 18.1.

Suppose $(S^{3},g)$ and $h$ satisfy the constraints (18.1) and $\int_{S^{3}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}_{g}\geq 0$ . Then there is an open set $\Omega\subset S^{3}$ satisfying

- • $\mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega)=\omega_{1}(g,h)$ ,

- • $\partial\Omega$ is a disjoint union of smooth embedded spheres with prescribed mean curvature $h$ with respect to $\Omega$ .

Since reversing orientations corresponds to reversing the sign of $h$ , Theorems 1.5 and 1.7 follow from Theorem 18.1.

### 19. Density Estimates in the 3-Sphere

We exhibit an upper and lower bound for the mass of a min-max varifold for the $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ functional with a point of density at least two. We show that these two bounds are contradictory in the case of our chosen setup.

We first show an upper bound, using the upper bound for $c$ , the upper bound for the volume of $(S^{3},g)$ , and the lower bound for the scalar curvature of $g$ .

#### Proposition 19.1.

Suppose $(S^{3},g)$ satisfies the hypotheses of §18. Suppose $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}$ satisfies $\|V\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\leq\omega_{1}(g,h)$ . Then

$$ \|V\|(S^{3})\leq 4\pi+vc. $$

#### Proof.

Let $h_{+}:=\min\{0,h\}$ and $h_{-}:=\min\{0,-h\}$ . We compute

$$ \displaystyle\|V\|(S^{3})-\int_{S^{3}}h_{+}\ d\mathcal{H}^{3} \displaystyle\leq\|V\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3} \displaystyle\leq\omega_{1}(g,h) \displaystyle\leq\omega_{1}(g,0)+\int_{S^{3}}h_{-}\ d\mathcal{H}^{3} \displaystyle\leq 4\pi+\int_{S^{3}}h_{-}\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}, $$

where the inequality $\omega_{1}(g,0)\leq 4\pi$ follows from the assumptions $\Ric(g)>0$ and $R_{g}\geq 6$ by [MN12, Theorem 1.1]. Since $|h|\leq c$ and $\mathcal{H}^{3}(S^{3},g)\leq v$ , the conclusion follows. ∎

To prove the lower bound, we recall a monotonicity formula for the Willmore energy (modified for our setting).

#### Lemma 19.2 ([Sim93, (1.4)] and [Top98, §6]).

If $V$ is an integer rectifiable 2-varifold in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ with bounded first variation and finite mass, then

$$ \pi\Theta^{2}(V,x_{0})\leq\frac{1}{16}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{4}}|H_{V}|^{2}\ d\|V\| $$

for any $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ .

#### Proof.

We note that the proof given in the first part of the proof of Lemma 1 from [Top98] applies to varifolds (where our convention for mean curvature differs from Topping’s by a factor of 2). The only point where the $C^{1}$ assumption is used is in showing that the rightmost term in [Top98, (21)] vanishes as $\sigma\to 0$ . Instead, we use the more trivial bound:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{B_{\sigma}}(\sigma^{-2}-\rho^{-2})X\cdot H_{V}\ d\|V\| \displaystyle\leq((\sigma^{-2}-\rho^{-2})\sigma c)\|V\|(B_{\sigma}) \displaystyle\leq c\sigma\frac{\|V\|(B_{\sigma})}{\sigma^{2}}=O(\sigma) $$

as $\sigma\to 0$ by the monotonicity formula and assumption of bounded support and finite mass. ∎

We apply this monotonicity formula to obtain the mass lower bound.

#### Proposition 19.3.

Suppose $(S^{3},g)$ satisfies the hypotheses of §18. If $V$ is a varifold in $(S^{3},g)$ with $c$ -bounded first variation and $\Theta^{2}(V,x)\geq 2$ for some $x\in S^{3}$ , then

$$ \|V\|(S^{3})\geq\frac{8\pi}{(1+\kappa)^{2}+c^{2}/4}. $$

#### Proof.

Using the isometric embedding of $(S^{3},g)$ into $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ , we view $V$ as a 2-varifold in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$ . By the bound on the second fundamental form of $S^{3}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}$ , we have

$$ |H_{V}^{\mathbb{R}^{N}}|^{2}\leq 4(1+\kappa)^{2}+c^{2}. $$

By Lemma 19.2 and the assumption of a point of density at least 2, we have

$$ \displaystyle 2\pi\leq\frac{1}{16}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}|H_{V}^{\mathbb{R}^{N}}|^{2}\ d\|V\|\leq\frac{4(1+\kappa)^{2}+c^{2}}{16}\|V\|(S^{3}), $$

which yields the desired inequality. ∎

Combining the mass upper and lower bounds, we deduce the desired conclusion about the density of special varifolds appearing in the min-max construction.

#### Corollary 19.4.

Suppose $(S^{3},g)$ satisfies the hypotheses of §18. Suppose $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}$ satisfies $\|V\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}=\omega_{1}(g,h)$ . Further suppose that the varifold $V$ has integer density everywhere and $c$ -bounded first variation in $(S^{3},g)$ . Then $\Theta^{2}(V,x)=1$ for all $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose otherwise for contradiction. Then by Proposition 19.3 and Proposition 19.1, we must have

$$ 4\pi+vc\geq\frac{8\pi}{(1+\kappa)^{2}+c^{2}/4}. $$

This inequality contradicts (18.1). ∎

### 20. Min-Max Proof

We show that each step in [CDL03] and [DLP10] can be modified to work in our setting.

#### 20.1. Nontrivial width

The fact that $\omega_{1}(g,h)>0$ follows immediately from the isoperimetric inequality. By the assumption $\int_{S^{3}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\geq 0$ , $\omega_{1}(g,h)$ cannot be achieved by a trivial solution (meaning a min-max sequence whose limit satisfies $V=0$ and $\Omega\in\{S^{3},\varnothing\}$ ).

#### 20.2. Pull-tight

For completeness, we recall the ideas of [ZZ19, §4], [ZZ20, §5] in the setting of the pull-tight argument of [CDL03] (specifically, we follow §2 of the errata for [CDL03]).

Let $\mathbf{F}$ denote the varifold distance on $\mathcal{V}_{2}(S^{3},g)$ , the space of 2-varifolds in $(S^{3},g)$ .

Take $L=2(\omega_{1}(g,h)+c\mathrm{Vol}_{g}(S^{3}))$ 99 9 Recall that $|h|\leq c$ ., and let $A^{L}=\{V\in\mathcal{V}_{2}(S^{3},g)\mid\|V\|(S^{3})\leq 2L\}$ , which is compact in $\mathbf{F}$ .

Let $A^{c}_{\infty}=\{V\in A^{L}\mid|\delta V(X)|\leq c\int_{S^{3}}|X|d\mu_{V}\ \text{for all smooth vectors fields}\ X\}$ . By [ZZ19, Lemma 4.1], $A^{c}_{\infty}$ is a compact subset of $A^{L}$ in the $\mathbf{F}$ -topology.

For $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , define $A_{k}=\{V\in A^{L}\mid 2^{-k-2}\leq\mathbf{F}(V,A^{c}_{\infty})\leq 2^{-k+1}\}$ .

For each $V\in A_{k}$ (by the definition of $A^{c}_{\infty}$ ), there is a smooth vector field $X_{V}$ satisfying

$$ \delta V(X_{V})+c\int_{S^{3}}|X_{V}|d\mu_{V}<0\ \ \text{and}\ \ \|X_{V}\|_{C^{k}}\leq\frac{1}{k} $$

(the second condition can be guaranteed by scaling).

For each $V\in A_{k}$ , there is an $\mathbf{F}$ -metric ball $B_{\rho_{V}}^{\mathbf{F}}(V)$ so that

$$ \delta W(X_{V})+c\int_{S^{3}}|X_{V}|d\mu_{W}\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(\delta V(X_{V})+c\int_{S^{3}}|X_{V}|d\mu_{V}\right)<0 $$

for all $W\in B_{\rho_{V}}(V)$ .

By compactness, cover $A_{k}$ by finitely many such metric balls $B_{\rho_{i}}^{\mathbf{F}}(V_{i})$ . Let $\{\psi_{i}\}$ be a continuous partition of unity subordinate to the covering $\{B_{\rho_{i}}^{\mathbf{F}}(V_{i})\}$ , and define

$$ V\in A_{k}\mapsto H_{V}^{k}=\sum_{i}\psi_{i}(V)X_{V_{i}}. $$

Now choose $\Psi_{k}$ a compactly supported continuous function on $A_{k}$ with $0\leq\Psi_{k}\leq 1$ and $\Psi_{k}\equiv 1$ on $\{V\in A^{L}\mid 2^{-k-1}\leq\mathbf{F}(V,A^{c}_{\infty})\leq 2^{-k}\}\subset A_{k}$ . On $A^{L}\setminus A^{c}_{\infty}$ , define

$$ H_{V}=\frac{\sum_{k}\Psi_{k}(V)H_{V}^{k}}{\sum_{k}\Psi_{k}(V)}. $$

We can extend the map $V\mapsto H_{V}$ to $A^{c}_{\infty}$ with $H_{V}=0$ for $V\in A^{c}_{\infty}$ . Since $\|H_{V}\|_{C^{k}}\leq\frac{1}{k}$ if $\mathbf{F}(V,A^{c}_{\infty})\leq 2^{-k+1}$ by construction (by the choice of normalization of $X_{V}$ ), the extension is a continuous map to the $C^{\infty}$ topology on the space of smooth vector fields. Moreover, $H_{V}$ satisfies

$$ \delta V(H_{V})+c\int_{S^{3}}|H_{V}|d\mu_{V}<0 $$

for all $V\in A^{L}\setminus A^{c}_{\infty}$ .

The rest of the proof now follows [CDL03, Errata Proposition 2.1] exactly (normalizing the speed of the isotopies generated by the vector fields $H_{V}$ and smoothing the new sweepout), with the additional observation that the first variation of $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ satisfies

$$ \delta\mathcal{A}^{h}_{\Omega}(X)=\delta|\partial\Omega|(X)-\int_{S^{3}}h\langle X,\nu_{\partial\Omega}\rangle d\mu_{|\partial\Omega|}\leq\delta|\partial\Omega|(X)+c\int_{S^{3}}|X|d\mu_{|\partial\Omega|} $$

(for a sweepout $\{\Omega_{t}\}$ , the isotopies generated by the vector fields $H_{|\partial\Omega_{t}|}$ will be applied to the sets $\Omega_{t}$ ).

Hence, there is a minimizing sequence $\{\Omega_{t}^{j}\}$ with the property that every min-max sequence $\{\Omega_{t_{j}}^{j}\}$ satisfies $\mathbf{v}(\partial\Omega_{t_{j}}^{j})\rightharpoonup V$ for $V\in A^{c}_{\infty}$ .

#### 20.3. Almost-minimizing

We say $\Omega\subset S^{3}$ is $\varepsilon$ -almost minimizing in $U\subset S^{3}$ if there is no isotopy $\phi\in\mathcal{I}(U)$ satisfying

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(t,\Omega))\leq\mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega)+\varepsilon/8, $$

$$ \mathcal{A}^{h}(\phi(1,\Omega))\leq\mathcal{A}^{h}(\Omega)-\varepsilon. $$

We say a sequence $\{\Omega^{j}\}$ is almost minimizing in $U$ if $\Omega^{j}$ is $\varepsilon_{j}$ almost minimizing in $U$ with $\varepsilon_{j}\to 0$ .

With this definition, we see that the argument of [CDL03, §5] is general and does not depend on the specific choice of functional. Hence, there is a function $r:S^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{+}$ and a min-max sequence $\{\Omega^{j}\}$ satisfying the conclusions of (2) so that $\{\Omega^{j}\}$ is almost minimizing in any annulus centered at any $x\in S^{3}$ with outer radius at most $r(x)$ .

To allow application of our regularity theory, we assume (without loss of generality) that $\mathcal{H}^{3}(B_{r(x)}(x))\leq\eta/8$ for all $x\in M$ .

#### 20.4. Regularity of weak replacements

#### Definition 20.1.

Let $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}_{c}$ . A pair $(V^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}_{c}$ is a weak replacement for $(V,\Omega)$ in $U\subset S^{3}$ if

- • $V^{\prime}\llcorner G(M\setminus\overline{U},2)=V\llcorner G(M\setminus\overline{U},2)$ and $\Omega\setminus\overline{U}=\Omega^{\prime}\setminus\overline{U}$ ,

- • $|\|V\|(S^{3})-\|V^{\prime}\|(S^{3})|\leq c\mathcal{H}^{3}(U)$ ,

- • $\|V^{\prime}\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\leq\|V\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}$ ,

- • $(V^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime})$ is in the $C^{1,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}$ graphical closure of the set of weakly stable $h$ -surfaces in $U$ .

#### Lemma 20.2.

If there is a function $r:S^{3}\to\mathbb{R}$ so that $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}_{c}$ has a weak replacement in any annulus centered at any $x\in S^{3}$ with outer radius at most $r(x)$ , then $V$ is integer rectifiable and any tangent cone to $V$ at any $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ is an integer multiple of a plane.

#### Proof.

We observe that the same proof as [CDL03, Lemma 6.4] works in our setting.

Density lower bound. The monotonicity formula implies there is a constant $c_{2}$ so that

$$ \frac{\|V\|(B_{\sigma}(x))}{\pi\sigma^{2}}\leq\frac{c_{2}\|V\|(B_{\rho}(x))}{\pi\rho^{2}} $$

for any varifold $V$ with $c$ -bounded first variation, $x\in S^{3}$ , and $\sigma<\rho\ll 1$ . Let $r<r(x)$ sufficiently small. Let $(V^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime})$ be a replacement for $(V,\Omega)$ in $A(x,r,2r)$ . By the maximum principle of [Whi10], $V^{\prime}$ is not identically 0 on $A(x,r,2r)$ . Since $V^{\prime}\llcorner G(A(x,r,2r),2)$ is the varifold of a $C^{1,1}$ immersion, there is a $y\in A(x,r,2r)$ with $\Theta^{2}(V^{\prime},y)\geq 1$ . Then we have

$$ \frac{\|V\|(B_{4r}(x))}{16\pi r^{2}}\geq\frac{\|V^{\prime}\|(B_{4r}(x))}{16\pi r^{2}}-Cr\geq\frac{\|V^{\prime}\|(B_{2r}(y))}{16\pi r^{2}}-Cr\geq\frac{c_{2}}{4}-Cr. $$

Hence, we have a uniform positive lower bound for the density by taking $r$ sufficiently small. By [All72, Theorem 5.5], $V$ is rectifiable.

Tangent cones. Let $x\in\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ . Let $C$ be a tangent cone to $V$ at $x$ , and let $\rho_{n}\to 0$ satisfy

$$ (f_{x,\rho_{n}})_{\#}V\rightharpoonup C. $$

Let $(V_{n}^{\prime},\Omega_{n}^{\prime})$ be a replacement for $(V,\Omega)$ in $A(x,\rho_{n}/4,3\rho_{n}/4)$ . Let $W_{n}^{\prime}=(f_{x,\rho_{n}})_{\#}V_{n}^{\prime}$ . Up to a subsequence (not relabeled), we have $W_{n}^{\prime}\rightharpoonup C^{\prime}$ , where $C^{\prime}$ is a stationary varifold. By the definition of the replacement, we have

$$ C^{\prime}\llcorner G(B_{1}(0)\setminus A(0,1/4,3/4),2)=C\llcorner G(B_{1}(0)\setminus A(0,1/4,3/4),2), $$

$$ \|C^{\prime}\|(B_{\rho}(0))=\|C\|(B_{\rho}(0))\ \ \forall\ \ \rho\in(0,1/4)\cup(3/4,1). $$

Since $C$ is a cone, (20.1) implies

$$ \frac{\|C^{\prime}\|(B_{\sigma}(0))}{\pi\sigma^{2}}=\frac{\|C^{\prime}\|(B_{\rho}(0))}{\pi\rho^{2}} $$

for all $\rho\in(0,1/4)\cup(3/4,1)$ . By stationarity and monotonoicity, we conclude that $C^{\prime}$ is a cone. Since $C$ and $C^{\prime}$ agree on $B_{1/4}(0)$ , we have $C^{\prime}=C$ . By Theorem 17.3, the convergence in $A(0,1/4,3/4)$ is $C^{1,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}$ graphical. By the same argument as in the proof of Claims 1 and 2 in Theorem 17.3 (i.e. the mean curvature of each sheet vanishes in the limit, and the ordering of sheets is preserved so we can apply the strong maximum principle), $C^{\prime}$ is the varifold of a smooth embedded minimal surface with integer multiplicity on the annulus $A(0,1/4,3/4)$ . Then $C^{\prime}$ is (an integer multiple of) a smooth embedded minimal cone in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , and hence a plane with integer multiplicity. ∎

#### 20.5. Regularity of replacements

#### Definition 20.3.

Let $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}_{c}$ . A pair $(V^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime})\in\mathcal{P}_{c}$ is a replacement for $(V,\Omega)$ in $U\subset S^{3}$ if

- • $V^{\prime}\llcorner G(M\setminus\overline{U},2)=V\llcorner G(M\setminus\overline{U},2)$ ,

- • $|\|V\|(S^{3})-\|V^{\prime}\|(S^{3})|\leq c\mathcal{H}^{3}(U)$ ,

- • $\|V^{\prime}\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\leq\|V\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}$ ,

#### Remark 20.4.

Observe that any replacement is also a weak replacement.

#### Definition 20.5.

The pair $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}_{c}$ has the good replacement property if

- (1) there is a positive function $r:U\to\mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that there is a replacement $(V^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime})$ for $(V,\Omega)$ in any annulus centered at $x$ with outer radius at most $r(x)$ for all $x\in U$ ,

- (2) there is a positive function $r^{\prime}:U\to\mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that there is a replacement $(V^{\prime\prime},\Omega^{\prime\prime})$ for the replacement $(V^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime})$ from (1) in any annulus centered at $x$ with outer radius at most $r(x)$ and any annulus centered at $y$ with outer radius at most $r^{\prime}(y)$ for any $y\in U$ ,

- (3) there is a positive function $r^{\prime\prime}:U\to\mathbb{R}^{+}$ such that there is a replacement $(V^{\prime\prime\prime},\Omega^{\prime\prime\prime})$ for the replacement $(V^{\prime\prime},\Omega^{\prime\prime})$ from (2) in any annulus centered at $z$ with outer radius at most $r^{\prime\prime}(z)$ for any $z\in U$ .

#### Lemma 20.6.

If $(V,\Omega)\in\mathcal{P}_{c}$ has the good replacement property, then $V$ is an embedded smooth surface with prescribed mean curvature $h$ with respect to $\Omega$ .

#### Proof.

Since unique continuation and curvature estimates hold, the proof is the same as the proof of [CDL03, Proposition 6.3]. The only exception is the argument showing $\Sigma\subset\mathrm{spt}\|V\|$ on $B_{\rho}(x)\setminus\{x\}$ , which in [CDL03] uses that $\|V\|(S^{3})=\|V^{\prime}\|(S^{3})$ . Instead, we follow the argument from [ZZ19, Theorem 6.1 Claim 5] and [ZZ20, Theorem 7.1 Claim 5], which applies to our setting. ∎

#### 20.6. Construction of replacements

The construction in [CDL03, §7] is general and applies to our setting (see also [ZZ20, §6]). We need only make three observations.

First, to go from the regularity of minimizers in isotopy classes to the regularity of minimizers in constrained isotopy classes, we need a squeezing lemma like [CDL03, Lemma 7.4]. We note that the same proof applies in our setting, as volume changes after squeezing will be arbitrarily small.

Second, since the weak replacement is constructed as the limit of solutions to constrained minimization problems for $\mathcal{A}^{h}$ , the inequality

$$ \|V^{\prime}\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}\leq\|V\|(S^{3})-\int_{\Omega}h\ d\mathcal{H}^{3}=\omega_{1}(g,h) $$

for the weak replacement $(V^{\prime},\Omega^{\prime})$ of the pair $(V,\Omega)$ from (18.2) follows immediately.

Finally, we observe that the replacements constructed in this way are a priori only weak replacements. However, the pull-tight argument, Lemma 20.2, (20.2), and Corollary 19.4 imply that the weak replacements we construct are in fact strong replacements under the assumptions of Theorem 18.1.

#### 20.7. Genus bound

We follow the argument of [DLP10].

The analogue of [DLP10, Proposition 3.2], i.e. regularity of the constrained isotopy minimization problem, follows from the above interior and boundary regularity theorems, combined with the observation that the squeezing argument at the boundary from [DLP10, Lemma 6.1] works in our setting (after squeezing, volume changes will be arbitrarily small).

The proof of [DLP10, Proposition 2.1] in [DLP10, §4] follows the same argument combined with the following observations. First, the min-max limit $V$ is a smooth embedded surface of prescribed mean curvature and satisfies unique continuation. Hence, when we solve local constrained minimization problems and take limits using the compactness theory developed in Part III, the apriori $C^{1,1}$ local minimizers converge in $C^{1,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}$ to the smooth limit $V$ . Since local minimizers are smooth where they have density 1, we can always take the local constrained minimizers to be smooth stable embedded surfaces of prescribed mean curvature. Second, the estimate [DLP10, Lemma 4.2] holds for smooth surfaces with bounded mean curvature, where the constant $C$ depends on the mean curvature bound. The proof follows by keeping track of the nonvanishing left hand side in the first variation formula [DLP10, (A.2)].

Equipped with Simon’s Lifting Lemma [DLP10, Proposition 2.1], the rest of the proof is identical.

### Appendix A Maximum Principle

A maximum principle is required to patch together the limits of decomposed stacked disk minimization problems. Since we obtain lower regularity than in the minimal surface setting, we need a maximum principle in the setting of $C^{1,\alpha}$ surfaces.

We adopt the following definition from [ZZ19].

#### Definition A.1.

Let $N_{i}$ ( $i=1,2$ ) be connected embedded two-sided $C^{1}$ surfaces in a connected open subset $W\subset M$ with $\partial N_{i}\cap W=\varnothing$ . Let $\nu_{i}$ be the unit normal to $N_{i}$ . We say that $N_{2}$ lies on one side of $N_{1}$ if $N_{1}$ divides $W$ into two connected components $W_{1}\cup W_{2}=W\setminus N_{1}$ , where $\nu_{1}$ points into $W_{1}$ and either:

- • $N_{2}\subset\overline{W_{1}}$ , which we write as $N_{1}\leq N_{2}$ ; or

- • $N_{2}\subset\overline{W_{2}}$ , which we write as $N_{1}\geq N_{2}$ .

#### Lemma A.2 (Maximum Principle).

Let $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ be $C^{1,\alpha}$ surfaces in a connected open set $W$ so that $N_{1}$ lies on one side of $N_{2}$ , $N_{1}\geq N_{2}$ , $N_{2}\geq N_{1}$ , and $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ intersect tangentially at $x\in W$ . If each $N_{i}$ has nonnegative mean curvature in the weak sense with respect to the normal $\nu_{i}$ , then $N_{1}=N_{2}$ and each is a smooth minimal surface.

#### Proof.

Since the unit normals point in opposite directions, being smooth and minimal follows if we show $N_{1}=N_{2}$ .

Suppose for contradiction $N_{1}\neq N_{2}$ . Without loss of generality, there is a sequence $x_{j}\to x$ with $x_{j}\in N_{1}\setminus N_{2}$ . Let $P\subset T_{x}M$ be the common tangent plane of $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ at $x$ , and let $\nu=\nu_{1}(x)$ be a unit normal to $P$ , so that $\nu_{2}(x)=-\nu$ . Let $r_{0}\in(0,1)$ be sufficiently small so that $\phi_{x}^{-1}(N_{1}\cap B_{r}^{M}(x))$ and $\phi_{x}^{-1}(N_{2}\cap B_{r_{0}}^{M}(x))$ are $C^{1,\alpha}$ graphs over $B\subset P$ , given by $C^{1,\alpha}$ functions $u_{1}\geq u_{2}$ and let $\rho\in(0,r_{0}/2)$ . Let $B_{r}$ denote $B^{\mathbb{R}^{2}}_{r}(0)$ .

We shall use the same setup as in the proof of Proposition 11.1. We let

- • $\tilde{g}$ be the rescaled pullback metric $(\phi_{x}\circ\mu_{\rho})^{*}g$ , so that

$$ \|\tilde{g}-g_{\text{Euc}}\|_{C^{\infty}(B_{2}\times[-1,1])}\leq\delta(\rho), $$

where $\delta(\rho)\to 0$ as $\rho\to 0$ ;

- • $\tilde{u}_{i}:B_{2}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $\tilde{u}_{i}(x)=\rho^{-1}u_{i}(\rho x)$ so that

$$ \|\tilde{u}_{i}\|_{C^{1}(B_{2})}\leq\delta(\rho); $$

- • $A(x,z,p)$ be such that with the rescaled metric $\tilde{g}$ on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ , we have $\mathcal{H}^{2}(\text{graph }u|_{B_{r}})=\int_{B_{r}}A(x,u,Du)\ dx$ for all $C^{1}$ functions $u:B_{2}\to\mathbb{R}$ and $r\in(0,2)$ ;

- • $Q$ be the mean curvature operator for graphs over $B_{2}$ with respect to $\tilde{g}$ .

Then $Q(u)\leq 0$ (resp. $\geq 0$ ) in the weak sense in $B_{1}$ is equivalent to (in our choice of sign convention)

$$ \int_{B_{1}}(A_{p}(x,u,Du)\cdot D\phi+A_{z}(x,u,Du)\phi)\leq 0\ (\text{resp. }\geq 0) $$

for all $\phi\in W^{1,2}_{0}(B_{1})$ with $\phi\geq 0$ .

By assumption, we have $Q(\tilde{u}_{1})\geq 0$ and $Q(\tilde{u}_{2})\leq 0$ in the weak sense. If we let $v=\tilde{u}_{1}-\tilde{u}_{2}\geq 0$ , then $v\in C^{1,\alpha}$ is a non-negative weak supersolution of a linear elliptic equation with continuous coefficients (depending on $\tilde{u}_{1}$ and $\tilde{u}_{2}$ ) as in [GT01, Theorem 10.7], i.e.

$$ \int_{B_{1}}(a^{ij}D_{j}v+b^{i}v)D_{i}\phi-(-b^{i}D_{i}v+cv)\phi\geq 0 $$

for all non-negative $\phi\in W_{0}^{1,2}(B_{1})$ , where $\tilde{u}_{t}=t\tilde{u}_{1}+(1-t)\tilde{u}_{2}$ and

$$ \displaystyle a^{ij} \displaystyle\coloneqq\int_{0}^{1}A_{p_{i}p_{j}}(x,\tilde{u}_{t},D\tilde{u}_{t})\ dt \displaystyle b^{i} \displaystyle\coloneqq\int_{0}^{1}A_{p_{i}z}(x,\tilde{u}_{t},D\tilde{u}_{t})\ dt \displaystyle c \displaystyle\coloneqq-\int_{0}^{1}A_{zz}(x,\tilde{u}_{t},D\tilde{u}_{t})\ dt. $$

Since $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ intersect tangentially at $x$ , $v(0)=0$ , and $\inf_{B_{1/4}}v=0$ . Hence, the weak Harnack inequality for supersolutions [GT01, Theorem 8.18] implies $\|v\|_{L^{1}(B_{1/2})}=0$ . As $v$ is $C^{1,\alpha}$ , this means $v|_{B_{1/2}}\equiv 0$ , contradicting the choice of the sequence $x_{j}\to x$ . ∎
